subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AND WELLAND CANAL   STATEMENT ON TOLL INCREASES

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AND WELLAND CANAL   STATEMENT ON TOLL INCREASES
speechtext:
As I indicated to the right hon. gentleman opposite yesterday, I am in a position now to give a very brief statement about tolls on the St. Lawrence seaway. I am making the statement now because parliament, we rather hope, may be in adjournment for a little while and certain things may have to happen during the adjournment. I should like the house to know what may take place.
The St. Lawrence seaway authority has advised me that the authority and the St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation of the United States expect shortly to reach tentative agreement on a notice to be published for the purpose of public hearings on the subject of the review of seaway tolls. This notice will be issued as soon as it is available.
On December 23, 1963, the government of Canada and the government of the United States exchanged notes agreeing to repeal the suspension of tolls on the Welland canal effective April 1, 1964. The result of this action would have been to restore the level of tolls as they were established in 1959 by the previous administration.
The government has now decided not to reimpose the tolls on the Welland canal at the present time. Accordingly, Canada and the United States have agreed to exchange further notes to withhold the reimposition of Welland canal tolls, and in doing so the government reserved its freedom of action to meet future developments.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AND WELLAND CANAL   STATEMENT ON TOLL INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this action on the part of the government is most commendable. This is another example of retreat by this government. In December, with precipitate haste, they rushed in to announce that Welland canal tolls, which we had removed, were going to be reimposed on April 1. They have had to retreat from that position. I know everyone will be very happy that the

government has once more followed the policy of the administration of which I had the honour to be the leader.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AND WELLAND CANAL   STATEMENT ON TOLL INCREASES
speechtext:
We are
pleased, Mr. Speaker, that a decision has been made not to reimpose tolls at this time. However, the minister gave no indication of something that has been linked with the whole question of tolls, and that is the idea of the twinning of the canal and the financing of both the seaway and the proposed twinning. It seems to me that he might have gone so far in his statement as to give us something of this background material. I think he would have to agree that since there has been no ruling, and since he reserved the right of the government to reimpose tolls on some future occasion, we still have what you might call a lobbying or pressure situation upon all parties. I know the minister will regret this as much as anyone else, and that is the reason I think we should expect, either today or in the near future, an enlarged statement taking into account the financial position of the St. Lawrence seaway authority and the expenditures for twinning the canal.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question arising out of the comment that has appeared on the very long answer he gave on Tuesday in connection with the refusal of United States subsidiary companies to ship automotive parts to China. speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: REPORTED REFUSAL OF U.S. SUBSIDIARY COMPANIES TO SHIP TO CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am most grateful to the hon. member for Port Arthur for relieving me of the necessity of raising a question of privilege. As I understood the front page story in the Toronto Globe and Mail this morning, Mr. Grinkus of the Gain Import Company is charging me with misleading the house, and he has charged me with telling a lie.
May I read what I said as recorded at page 1398 of Hansard for March 24. The particular charge Mr. Grinkus has made, according to the newspaper article, is that I had denied I had received complaints from his company, and I should like to read what I said on Tuesday. The hon. member for Bumaby-Coquit-lam asked me a question; first, if I had received any complaints from Canadian exporters with regard to the refusal of automobile companies in Canada which are subsidiaries of United States automobile manufacturers to supply automotive parts to China. This was my reply:
As I said yesterday, I was unaware of any complaints but I found that last summer I had received a complaint from one exporter, whose name I believe was Mr. Ginkus-

Perhaps he was annoyed because Hansard misspelled his name, which should have been "Grinkus".
-of Gain Import Company Limited, who was unable to obtain a supply of certain types of automotive parts for export to mainland China.
It is clear from Hansard that I did refer specifically to the complaint he registered.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question I might read a short statement on the current situation in Cyprus.
General Gyani, who has been designated by the secretary general as commander of the United Nations peace keeping force, has now arrived in Cyprus from Geneva. As has been reported in the press, the Secretary of State for External Affairs had an opportunity to hold detailed discussions with General Gyani in Geneva concerning the operational role which the peace keeping force will undertake on the island. We understand that the advance party of the Swedish contingent will arrive in Cyprus today, to be followed shortly by elements of the Finnish and Irish contingents. Consequently it is expected that the secretary general will inform the security council, possibly tomorrow, that the United Nations force has become operational.
Yesterday it was announced that the Finnish ambassador to Sweden, Sakari Tuomioja, has been named by the secretary general as United Nations mediator on Cyprus. The governments of Cyprus, Greece, Turkey and Great Britain have agreed to the nomination of Mr. Tuomioja, and after consultations with the United Nations secretariat in New York this week end he is expected to arrive in Cyprus the middle of next week.
Inquiries of the Ministry
With respect to the terms of reference under which Mr. Tuomioja will carry out his functions on Cyprus, these were broadly defined in the security council resolution adopted on March 4. The relevant portion of the resolution calling for the appointment of a mediator reads as follows:
The security council recommends further that the secretary general designate, in agreement with the government of Cyprus and the governments of Greece. Turkey and the United Kingdom, a mediator, who shall use his best endeavours with representatives of the communities and also with the aforesaid four governments, for the purpose of promoting a peaceful solution and an agreed settlement of the problem confronting Cyprus, in accordance with the charter of the United Nations, having in mind the well-being of the people of Cyprus as a whole and the preservation of international peace and security. The mediator shall report periodically to the secretary general on his efforts.
Thus it is apparent that the mediator is to be directly responsible to the secretary general. As in the case of the United Nations force, any directives from the secretary general to the force commander and additional information concerning the terms of reference for the mediator may be expected to be made known to the countries contributing to the United Nations force. However, the secretary general has made it clear that he does not feel it is in the best interests of law and order on the island for promoting a peaceful solution to make public details of the terms of reference.
It is apparent that the presence of the Canadian contingent as part of the United Nations peace keeping force on Cyprus has had a calming effect on the island. It is hoped that this influence will continue after the United Nations force becomes operational and elements of this force replace certain British forces who have been keeping the peace throughout the island. With the presence of the United Nations force commander on Cyprus and the anticipated arrival of the mediator within a few days, the task of maintaining and restoring law and order will commence, which it is hoped will make it possible for discussions to begin on seeking ways and means of bringing about reconciliation between the two communities.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON USE OF SYMBOL DELETED BY PARLIAMENT FROM BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised last Tuesday that he would make inquiries and reply to questions that had been raised about the emblem for the world exhibition. The Prime Minister has made these inquiries and has asked me to say that the corporation has made the following explanation.
First, the question of the emblem has been on the agenda of the board of directors since March 19, 1963. The emblem which was confirmed on March 13, 1964 had first been adopted by the board at a meeting held on August 12, 1963, under the chairmanship of the previous commissioner general, Mr. Bien-venu. The corporation registered its copyright in the emblem with the copyright office in Ottawa as early as August 28, 1963.
Second, the choice of the emblem is the responsibility of the board of directors. When the emblem was originally adopted, the board instructed the management to seek maximum legal protection for it in respect of both copyright and trade mark. As existing legislation in these fields could not provide the corporation with the full protection it needed, an amendment to this effect to the incorporating act was requested. Obviously the purpose of the amendment was not to seek the approval of parliament for the emblem itself, but rather to obtain the additional legal protection for it that was considered necessary. I might add that the government, for its part, has never assumed that it had any responsibility for the choice of the emblem itself.
Third, the amendment finally adopted by the house states that "any symbol adopted by the corporation not later than December 31, 1964, is hereby declared to be the official symbol of the exhibition, as of the date of its publication in the Canada Gazette". The board of directors has interpreted this provision as allowing it, after giving due consideration to the views which were expressed in the house on December 20, 1963, to confirm the emblem if, in its best judgment, the board continued to regard it as the most suitable one.
Fourth, the board has made every effort to secure the best artistic advice available, both before the original adoption of the emblem on August 12, 1963 and before its confirmation on March 13, 1964. As a result of the criticisms made in the house early in January, the corporation established a subcommittee of its fine arts committee to re-examine the whole problem of the emblem. The subcommittee
14S4

Inquiries of the Ministry was under the chairmanship of Mr. Evan H. Turner and consisted of Mrs. Baillargeon of Montreal, Mr. Paul Arthur of Ottawa and Mr. J. C. Parkin of Toronto. The subcommittee held a number of meetings and reviewed all the symbols previously submitted to the corporation. It came to the unanimous conclusion that the design created by Mr. Julien Hebert was the most successful.
Fifth, the board, on the suggestion of the subcommittee, gave consideration to the advisability of holding a national competition to be conducted on a professional basis to select a new symbol. Since 184 different symbols had already been considered by the corporation, the board came to the view that a national competition was not likely to produce a symbol that would receive a greater measure of general support or would be less exposed to criticism than the present one.
Finally, the corporation has already received well over 100 requests from individuals or firms to be licensed for the immediate use of the symbol of the exhibition for commercial purposes, with offers of royalties in favour of the corporation. These offers have had to be withheld pending a definitive decision on the emblem, with a consequent loss of appreciable revenues to the corporation.
These are the reasons which have led the corporation to confirm the symbol. It is very understandable that members who dislike the symbol should feel impelled to express their disappointment in the corporation's decision. It seems to me, however, and to the Prime Minister that the assertion that the corporation's action constitutes an affront to the rights of parliament is, in the circumstances, a matter of subjective judgment.
In view of the decision taken by the house last December, which protected any symbol rather than a particular one, and notwithstanding the condemnation of a particular symbol by many members at that time, the directors acted within the powers conferred on them in confirming their earlier decision.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer briefly to the problem raised yesterday by the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume).
In the second report it submitted in 1961, the joint committee on Indian affairs recommended that negotiations be undertaken between the federal government and the provinces for the eventual transfer of certain Eskimo affairs to the provinces. The committee also set out the standards which should be adopted in the future if such a transfer ever became a reality. It further stated that this action should be agreeable to the Indian population and, in the case with which we are concerned, to the Eskimo population, the provinces and the central government.
The matters in question come fundamentally, in my opinion, under the provincial jurisdiction, for instance, education and the development of human resources, under which falls the question of schools and education for the Eskimos. As a matter of fact, schools coming under the provincial jurisdiction were mentioned, as well as health and social welfare.
Mr. Chairman, one must realize that the present talks deal exclusively with an administrative transfer. It is not, and it is good to remember that, a legal or constitutional transfer because, in my opinion, such a transfer, as stated the other day by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), could not be made legally or constitutionally except through an amendment to the British North America Act.
It will be remembered that in 1912, by virtue of chapter 45 of the statutes of Canada, the federal government yielded to the province of Quebec its jurisdiction over the vast area known as New Quebec, Ungava and Rupert's Land, including the area of the Great Whale river. On the other hand, jurisdiction over the Indians living in these areas remained with Ottawa. This situation was confirmed in 1939 by the Supreme Court of 20220-95
Interim Supply
Canada, when it was asked by the federal government to determine which of the federal or the provincial governments should have jurisdiction in the matter.
In that judgment the supreme court held that, for jurisdiction purposes, Eskimos were on the same footing as Indians, and came under federal jurisdiction by virtue of section 91, paragraph 24, of the British North America Act, which gives the federal government authority on Indian affairs and the land reserved for them.
However, in order to satisfy the desire expressed in the report of the joint committee on Indian affairs, discussions had been instituted between the federal and provincial authorities, and I submit that those conversations-if they have any meaning, at all- have been instituted in order to give the province of Quebec the right to exercise a legitimate jurisdiction in a field for which it is responsible, over people living in a part of its territory.
Now, this being said, the committee must ask itself what standards any possible agreement will have to follow. First of all, such an agreement must take place, but up to now, and this has been somewhat confirmed by what the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) said this morning, it seems that the discussions with regard to the agreement have dragged on.
There is no doubt about that, for the minister said that since February 29, not a single meeting was held between the federal and provincial authorities to discuss the matter.
That is why we must respect the wishes of those people and first think of their interest when a solution is adopted.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that Quebec will want to preserve in its entirety the culture, the language and all the human values which the Eskimos represent for Quebec and Canada.
I must tell you that the Eskimos themselves are aware of their contribution to Canadian culture and, on other hand, of the fact that they are members of the great human race. That is why they like to call themselves "Inutuinaq" which, in their language, means "man".
It is at this higher level that we must consider the problem.
The minister said vaguely that there had been discussions, but this boils down to very little and, in any case, would have no bearing on the final solution of that problem.
Another rule, which was said to be essential, must be followed. And it meets the views of the committee. It is that the Eskimos should be consulted on their own destiny. I completely agree that those people, citizens of our country, who were among the very first

Interim Supply
inhabitants of our continent, have the right to be consulted and that, in a very effective manner, as to the steps to be taken concerning them.
I say this because, on the one hand, the Eskimos already have the right to vote in a federal election and they exercise that right in a proportion of 80 per cent of their eligibility. Besides, it is an admitted right of any nation or of any group of individuals to determine their own system or way of life.
We all know that this right to self-determination is recognized by the United Nations charter and must apply to any nation. That right is recognized by the Canadian Bill of Rights which was passed by this parliament, and also by the United Nations universal declaration on human rights.
In short, I am convinced that for those who live in the province of Quebec, the right of self-determination cannot be questioned. If there is a group in this country which should keep that right for itself and all the others, it is the people of the province of Quebec.
I therefore think that any federal-provincial agreement should consider the wishes of the Eskimos themselves.
Finally, I submit that the sovereignty of this parliament should be taken into account. To my mind, the final decision in this transfer of jurisdiction should be ratified by the federal parliament, in the same way, I suppose, as the agreement will be submitted to the Quebec legislature.
Finally, the problem and its solution should be integrated into the larger issue of an eventual transfer of jurisdiction over all Indians-a much wider problem of a constitutional nature, which concerns not only the federal authorities and the province of Quebec, but also most, if not all, other provinces in this country.
Therefore, we, on this side of the house, would like to have from the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) as well as from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) a clear and straightforward statement with regard to that agreement as well as to the demands of the federal government in its talks and negotiations with the province of Quebec.
So far, no clearcut statements have been made either by the minister of northern affairs or the Minister of Justice, not to mention the Prime Minister himself, on this matter. It would appear, judging by the replies given to the many questions raised about that on this side of the house, that there is a rather wide difference of opinion between the two ministers chiefly concerned, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources on one side and the Minister of Justice on the other.

That would naturally indicate the existence of more serious difficulties which could raise doubts as to the solidarity or the unity of views that the cabinet ought to show concerning any question, but especially the one now before us.
This is why I ask either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, provided that the latter makes it clear that he is speaking on behalf of the cabinet as he should normally do, to set forth the guiding principles under which the transfer will take place.
As for myself, Mr. Chairman, while I am not personally acquainted with the Eskimo, as the member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) who spoke yesterday, since I did not have the opportunity of travelling in those areas or living with Eskimos, I feel that the advantages of an administrative transfer to the province of Quebec are unquestionable; they are completely evident and obvious to everyone, and for the following reasons.
First, the matters to be transferred come essentially under provincial jurisdiction, such as education, health; those are matters of local interest in an area entirely located within the territory of the province of Quebec.
On the other hand, I am inclined to believe that once the transfer is effected, it would not be impossible that the province of Quebec would set up constituencies for those people, thus giving them full franchise. I would even consider the possibility that they could elect to the legislature a representative of Eskimo extraction. It is not impossible either that such a representative should also be elected to the federal parliament.
Mr. Chairman, we are faced with what is primarily a human problem, namely the disposal of human beings which are part of an alert people gifted with a sharp mind and artistic talents, who have, in fact, created an art of their own which is recognized throughout the world. These people have shown and continue to show that they are the depositaries of a native culture which is theirs alone and which substantially adds to our Canadian culture.
Mr. Chairman, let us respect the wish of the Eskimos. Let us respect their deep desire to remain themselves and let there be, before any final decision is taken, consultation absolutely free of pressure.
I think that in this perspective it would be normal that the Eskimos chose to be administered by the authorities of the province in which they live, that is the province of Quebec. Personally, I am sure that that government will preserve intact the value which the Eskimo people represent to the whole of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to commend the hon. member tor a moderate and very sensible speech on this subject. Did I understand the hon. member to say that he saw the eventual transfer of all Indian peoples to the provinces as natural and inevitable?

Mr. Chairman, I can assure the committee that before I decided to speak on this matter I did consider the question of the rules, and I would have hesitated to interrupt a discussion of such an important matter as we have been discussing did I not think that the matter which I proposed to raise was one of considerable urgency and that the opportunities to raise it were relatively limited. For this reason I propose to raise it now.
The subject I want to discuss at this moment and call to the attention of the government is, as I have said, in my view a matter of grave urgency, not only to my own constituents and to all constituents of the metropolitan area of Toronto but to very many people outside that area. I refer to the acute crisis caused by the lack of hospital beds in that area and the degree of responsibility which I believe falls upon this government to assist in remedying that situation. The existence and gravity of this crisis has been fully documented in the press. A report of a special committee of the Ontario hospital services commission estimated the need for hospital beds in that area at 2,360. Two of the hospitals in Toronto, out of three, have no emergency beds even for those who are in danger of dying. It takes from three weeks to two months at least to find accomodation for painful illnesses such as hernia and gallstones.
I have in front of me a news story which appeared in the Toronto daily Star of yesterday under the following heading, "Babies' lives at stake in hospital bed crisis-M.D." I read a brief extract from this report:
Metro's critical hospital bed shortage is risking children's lives.
This is the warning of Dr. Harvey Agnew, director of a study sponsored by the Ontario hospital services commission.
Dr. Agnew, in case hon. members of this house do not know this, is no person to speak lightly. He retired in 1961 as head of hospital administration of the University of Toronto. This is what the report says:
He said-
This is referring to Dr. Agnew:
-the acute shortage of suburban hospital beds for children endangers the lives of emergency and some newborn cases.
Hospital officials and doctors agreed the "situation is serious and additional beds in fairly substantial numbers must be provided shortly", he said.
I do not intend to go on and recount to the committee the numerous illustrations of this urgent need. I could do that at length
[The Deputy Chairman.]
but, as I have said, they have been fully brought out in the press. This is a problem which is particularly serious for older people in that many of them who are suffering from serious illness and should be in hospital are kept waiting two or three months before they can get a hospital bed.
The matter has reached the stage that the provincial government-in this particular field I would say that the federal government is the junior partner-has been accused of fraud in accepting money for hospital services which they are not in a position to provide after receiving the money for them. This matter has been under consideration by the federal government since October or November of last year. At that time the executive of the metropolitan council made representations to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and other ministers, including the Minister of Finance whom I am glad to see in the house at this moment. In these representations it was urged that the federal government should, in line with the increased grants already made by the provincial government and those made by the metropolitan area government, increase its present grant of $2,000 per bed. In fact, if I recall aright, I think it was suggested that the federal government should double its grant. The grant of $2,000 for hospital bed construction has not been increased in over a decade with the result that the level of federal grants has not kept pace with rising costs.
On the 3rd of December last year, I believe, I questioned the Minister of National Health and Welfare as to what reply she was going to give to the request of the executive of the metropolitan council in this matter. She said then that the matter was under active consideration. My colleague, the hon. member for Danforth, and myself have continued to question the minister and latterly the Prime Minister with regard to what decision the government has reached on this matter. So far we have had no definite answer. We are still told that the matter is under active consideration.
In my respectful view, Mr. Chairman, this is not merely a local matter. People from all over the province of Ontario and, indeed, from outside the province of Ontario avail themselves of the services of these hospitals. Nor is it merely an economic matter. There is a moral obligation of leadership upon the federal government. It is perfectly true that under our constitution the provision of hospitals is essentially a provincial responsibility, but the federal government in the past has recognized its share of responsibility and the necessity for giving leadership in this field.

I want to touch on a political note in this regard. In the last federal election the Liberal party, as is well known, swept the metropolitan area of Toronto and succeeded in electing members from all but the two constituencies represented by your humble member now speaking and the hon. member for Danforth. There are in fact in the metropolitan area of Toronto more members of parliament and electors than in seven out of the ten provinces of this country. I am aware that in the rest of Canada Toronto is not the most popular section of our country-

Mr. Chairman, in the discussion on interim supply, we are authorized to draw the members' attention to various matters which are of interest to us all. I therefore would like to start by mentioning a program which was televised yesterday on the English network of the C.B.C., under the title: "The Open Grave".
Mr. Chairman, the comments which this program gave rise to illustrate a point which we have been trying to bring to the attention of the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) for some time, to the effect that it might be appropriate, and even necessary, to set up a committee of the house to consider certain programs presented by the C.B.C. which is a crown corporation.
To my mind, it might be important to have such a committee to study those matters, for several reasons.
First of all, the C.B.C. might benefit by knowing the point of view of hon. members. As a matter of fact, we are constantly in contact with the people and we might convey the people's opinion to that crown corporation.
Yesterday, I listened to the telecast entitled: "The Open Grave". I wonder why there was so much fuss and noise made about that show. Personally, I saw nothing sacrilegious or scandalous.
There might have been a somewhat indirect reference in the scene where disciples of Mr. Corbett were shown, one of them betraying him. There was the allegory of the open grave. But possibly nothing scandalous or sacrilegious.
However, I must say, our attention having been called to such a play, that I expected worse than that. In my opinion the literary style was very poor, there were leitmotivs which by the end became boring. The vocabulary was very poor, and this play was certainly not a first class drama, far from it.
In my opinion, what saved the play some value was the excellence of the artists interpreting this drama, or at least what has been called a drama, as well as the excellence of the producers.
Now, as concerns the substance of this so-called dramatic play, I think the C.B.C. may be somewhat criticized, for it meant to convey a certain idea.
I consider this corporation as an agency not to be influenced or subjugated by politics. Therefore, that agency should not endeavour to convey some ideologies or political messages.

The substance of that play-at the beginning, I mostly discussed its form-carried a unilateral message resting on erroneous premises and, because of the style of the play, was beside the point.
There was an attempt to impress on the public a widely fashionable tendency in this country recently, and that was done with pressure when, for instance, interviews were carried out on the street where a consonant image or character was given of those approving the leader, while a clearly unlikable character was given to those against the leader of the "Peace in Action" movement, like the character who would not go on strike with the other demonstrators around a war plant. On the evening of Mr. Corbett's hanging, we could see motorcyclists waiting at the jail door and those characters were clearly antipathetic, once again to try to influence the public.
An attempt was made to ridicule the efficiency of the R.C.M.P., as it is done sometimes in this house. An attempt was made to ridicule the efficiency of our judicial institutions.
When such an argument is presented, people should at least have the decency to mention that it is a theory and not a theatrical work. I think it was done with such naivete that for a long time, the people fell for that sort of program. The author of that play gave me the impression of being a commercial publicist rather than a theatrical author who is trying to push through a philosophy, rather than attempting to present a theatrical work.
When we consider the amount of money the C.B.C. had to pay for such poor work- in French, we usely call that a turnip and it means something neither bad nor good, but something insipid-as the one shown on T.V. last night, I begin to wonder whether it would not be better for the corporation to appear before a committee of the house in order to receive suggestions.
As far as I am concerned, I do not object to appropriations, even large appropriations, for an agency like the C.B.C. which has work to do and can be a most important institution for the broadcasting of ideas and thoughts aimed at the development of art in Canada as well as understanding between the two main groups of this country. I have no objection to even larger appropriations.
If the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation finds insufficient the $85 million voted by the parliament of Canada, let us give it more, but its work should be at least well done and the money spent in a sensible way.
I am convinced that over the French network, between 80 and 85 per cent of expenses

are sensible ones. The majority of plays produced by the C.B.C. during the last five or six years have been successful. But in other cases, perhaps there is a lack of money or inefficient people in some positions. In any event, there is certainly need for an investigation in that regard.
Far be it from me to blame the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. On the contrary, I believe that the corporation, in the field of the theatre, for instance, as well as in the sport and language fields, is doing work of a high social order which helps the advancement and progress of the arts, culture and sport in this country.
However, there comes a time when it may need some advice or information. Then again, we could be the ones to require information on what is going on inside that crown corporation. That is why we believe it would be important and essential now to set up a committee of the house to study those problems. The fact that we are now in full evolution makes it all the more necessary.
I am less familiar with the English network, and I hope you will excuse me for that, because I do not have as many opportunities to watch it. True, I did watch it yesterday, but that was because I wanted to speak about a certain program.
I wish to congratulate the actors of the English network for their splendid performances, and I must not forget the producers who gave us a most beautiful play, even if its theme was more or less insignificant.
On the French network, we have very good performers and excellent producers, and if they need a bigger budget-

All that to say, Mr. Chairman, that hon. members would like to see a committee set up to examine the operation of the C.B.C.
Another point which is very important, in my opinion, is the question of federal-provincial relations which will be discussed next week in the historic city of Quebec. We hope that those talks will be followed by action and achievements and that changes will be made to keep pace with the present evolution.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to bring home another point. In view of the tendencies now existing in this country, in view of present conditions, the government must go to Quebec, to this federal-provincial conference, with the clear idea that it will hand back to the provinces as much as possible of certain sources of income, so that the provinces may look after themselves and solve their own problems themselves.
And here I would like to use an argument which was put forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) himself, in his budget speech, when he said that generally in the country as a whole, we have succeeded to settle the unemployment problem, since, by and large, it has declined. But, he admitted that the unemployment situation remained to be settled in some particular areas. In brief, while general measures have been beneficial in a general way, unemployment still remains a serious problem, since it has not been solved at the regional level. In other words, legislative centralization could succeed to check unemployment on the whole, but not to eradicate it in underdeveloped areas of the country, scattered all over the country, since there are 35 of those designated areas.
Centralized solutions have not helped settle the problem. On the contrary, and unemployment is a typical example. Now, it is intended to solve the problem of unemployment, and the Minister of Finance wants to solve it on a regional basis; but even in so doing, by legislating on a national basis, on a Canadian basis, for the country as a whole, in a standardized fashion, strictly general, without taking into account various regional characteristics, he cannot arrive at a solution to the problem of regional unemployment. The problem has not been solved because the measures were applied as a whole, and specific cases, in specific areas, were not considered. The problem has not been solved, because the solution was sought in a centralizing way, when it should be sought at the regional level.

It is to be noted that the winter works, in some areas, have not solved the problem, because some of those areas have weather conditions which do not make for an easy implementation of the general legislation, as it has been voted by Ottawa for the country as a whole. This means that the solution consists in favouring the decentralization of implementation methods, various solutions for various situations.
This is the proof that the remedies should differ according to different areas. This also underlines the necessity of decentralizing and turning over to the provinces the necessary sources of income so that they might bring about the required solutions.
Therefore, let us turn over the sources of income to the provinces, especially those faced with the greatest number of problems, such as the province of Quebec. Those factors should be kept in mind during the next federal-provincial conference to be held next week in Quebec city.
The province of Quebec is exceedingly rich at present and has a tremendous capacity for development, as well as all the manpower, engineers, scientists and technicians required to achieve this development. But the province is at a standstill; Quebec has 40 per cent of the unemployed of the country, because it is the victim of a way of thinking which is not its own, of an atmosphere which is not its own and because the given solutions do not satisfy the aspirations and characteristics of its people. Although Quebec has a tremendous potential development which would contribute to enrich the entire country, it remains underdeveloped, because it is not given the opportunity to apply its own methods of development, its own solutions according to its character, its way of thinking and its procedures.
These regional factors should be taken into account in the over-all economic solutions for the development of the country, exactly as the Minister of Finance must take them into consideration when a specific unemployment problem must be dealt with.
In such a case, I can assure the people of other areas that Quebec will do more than its share to co-operate with enthusiasm and with a deep sense of equality to the development of the whole country. But this means that Quebec must get back its sources of revenue, its rights so as to ensure its own development.
On the other hand, I entertain certain fears, and I mention them here because to give utterance to one's fears beforehand is sometimes the wise thing to do. I fear that the Prime Minister will arrive at the federal-provincial conference surrounded by advisers

who do not want to grasp the real meaning of the solutions to be found, who are blind to the real problems and their solutions.
I also fear that, on the other hand, the Quebec premier will take a sit-on-the-fence attitude at the federal-provincial conference, and take no real stand, as he did on April 5, 1963, three days before the last general election when he said: "We insist on a better distribution of revenue sources from the federal government, Quebec wants 100 per cent of the succession duties, 25 per cent of the corporation income tax and 25 per cent of the individual income tax."
By using that approach, he obtained the support of everybody. That was a year ago, or will be, in 15 days. Afterwards, the Quebec premier gave an ultimatum and we all got behind him.
He stated exactly the needs of the province of Quebec, what Quebec wants. He described clearly the requirements of the province of Quebec, so that it might really develop in this modern age.
Quebec was unanimous at that time and we must say to the premier of Quebec that we expect from him a very strong stand on those points, because any softening would result in a wave of disapproval on the part of the citizens of the province of Quebec.
Such a stand would discourage them, because they would understand that the premier of Quebec is not ready to do what he has been preaching for so long, namely give to the province of Quebec the means and the opportunity to become master in its own house, by developing itself to the advantage of all its citizens.
However, we do not want this to be done at the expense of the other provinces. We wish all regions of Canada, all Canadian citizens, to get the same opportunities, but we also wish the province of Quebec to get its own, and we feel that the country as a whole will profit by it, will make progress. The whole country will then take a step forward since when a part of the country is being developed, the other parts also profit by it.
Mr. Chairman, on the eve of this provincial conference, which will be extremely important, indeed strategic, we believe that the governments which will meet around the same table, the federal government and that of the nine other provinces, must look to the future, not in seeking to centralize everything in Ottawa, but in granting every province, every region, means and opportunities to develop themselves according to their own conditions.

I do not intend to take up too much time in this debate but I do have one or two things to say with respect to the proposed transfer of jurisdiction over the Eskimos living in northern Quebec from the federal government to the government of the province of Quebec.
In order that the situation may be put into proper perspective, I think I should refer to one or two things which have been said in this house by the Minister of Justice, by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. There seems to me to be as much difference between the minister of northern affairs and his cabinet colleagues, the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister, with respect to this question as there is between the Minister of Agriculture, if indeed he can still be called that, and the Minister of Forestry. The minister of northern affairs said on March 4 that there would be consultation with the Eskimos of northern Quebec before a transfer was effective-I think the words he used were "before an agreement is signed". As reported in Hansard of that date, the minister of northern affairs set forth the agreement, or rather the consensus of understanding, as he called it, between the representatives of the government of Quebec and the representatives of the government of Canada. In one of the conditions which was attached to this consensus of agreement, number four to be precise, which is recorded on page 506 of Hansard, it was stated that the government of Canada and Quebec undertake to consult jointly the Eskimos of New Quebec, or nouveau Quebec. The paragraph went on:
The consultation, that is the communication of the terms of the agreement, excluding the financial provisions thereof, and the receiving of the views and comments of the Eskimos concerned, would be made through a commission-
From what cabinet ministers have been telling us, it appears that agreement to set up this commission was reached between the two governments on February 29 last. This agreement was announced in the house by the minister of northern affairs on March 4. But as yet, according to the answer which the minister of northern affairs gave me this afternoon, there have been no further meetings between the representatives of the government of Quebec and the government of Canada in connection with this matter, nor has any progress been made toward the setting up of this commission.
It seems to me there can hardly be the kind of consultation which we have been led to believe will take place between the Eskimo people and the government of Canada if, as the minister says in the agreement which he 20220-96

put on record on March 4, the terms of reference of the commission provide merely- and I quote again from page 506 of Hansard- that consultation is to be only "the communication of the terms of the agreement", excluding the financial provisions. If this is what the hon. gentleman and the Prime Minister mean by consultation, it seems to me that the Eskimo people, 2,500 of them, will be presented with a fait accompli in the form of an agreement reached between the province of Quebec and the government of Canada. They will simply be informed that this is how things are to be. We have been urging that the Eskimo people should be consulted in the fullest sense of the term. It would appear that the fairest means of achieving this degree of consultation would be to invite representatives of the Eskimo people involved to serve as members of the commission which the two governments intend to set up and, in addition, to invite representatives of the Eskimos to express their views at any interim meetings held between the governments.
Here we have a situation where the minister of northern affairs, who is constitutionally and legally directly responsible for the welfare of these people, is entering into consultation with a provincial government, on behalf of the government of Canada, without having any regard whatsoever for the opinions and views of the Eskimos who are the subject of those consultations. The minister read into the record on March 4 the provisions of a consensus reached by the two governments, but there was no indication that the Eskimo people had been consulted as to the contents of even that concensus. It seems to me that the 2,500 Canadian citizens who are most directly involved should have been asked to express their views on the subject. They should have been asked to express their views as to the setting up of the commission. They should have been asked whether or not they wished to be represented on this commission. It seems to me it would have been fair to have done all these things rather than to have proceeded unilaterally, because of political pressure applied by the minister's cabinet colleagues the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, arbitrarily to transfer jurisdiction to the provincial government for purely political reasons.
I am not the only one who holds these views. One of the leading newspapers in this country, a paper to whose editorial policy I am sure those who sit on the government benches will not take exception, the Winnipeg Free Press, has called this whole matter an exercise in political appeasement, and that is precisely what it is. Here we have the

province of Quebec demanding, and indeed threatening, that the federal government turn over to it administrative responsibility for these people.
It is a responsibility which has been residing in the federal government, if not by the treaty of Paris of 1763, certainly from 1939 onwards. A decision was reached by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1939, at the insistence of the province of Quebec, that the responsibility for the welfare of the Eskimo people should reside in the federal government. In other words, the supreme court decided they would come within the classification of original people as contemplated by the Indian Act. From that time on the federal government has assumed the responsibility and I might say that during the years 1957 to 1963 the responsibility was discharged as never before in Canadian history.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the consultation which the minister of northern affairs and the Prime Minister have assured the house will be carried out is a very shallow device to hide the fact that it is the intention of the federal government to come to an agreement with the province of Quebec, and then hand that agreement as a fait accompli to the Eskimo people. Why has the government not considered Eskimo representation on the commission, and why does the government not ensure that independent counsel be provided both prior to the consideration of the terms of this so-called agreement and at the time the completed agreement is considered by the commission?
The minister of resources in Quebec said that it would be utterly undemocratic to hold a referendum on this question. The minister of resources in Quebec has been very outspoken on this subject. In some of the earlier meetings he said that unless the federal government follows the wishes of his province in this matter, they will not give the Eskimo people in northern Quebec jobs on provincial projects but rather will take residents from the central portion of the province and substitute their labour for the labour which is more readily available. Some newspaper commentators have called this blackmail. I hope that since the time when Mr. Levesque made this statement the federal officials involved, including the minister of northern affairs, have made some progress in bringing some modicum of rational thought to the minister of resources for Quebec.
The Eskimo people in this area are Canadian citizens and cannot be treated as human pawns, as appears to be the case. As the Leader of the Opposition stated the other day in this house, the Eskimo people are being treated as chattels in this transaction. They

are being shunted from pillar to post without regard to their feelings in the matter. The hon. member for Northwest Territories pointed out that he knew these people and how they feel, that they are fearful and confused. He further said that if the federal government insists on enforcing their views and on giving in to Quebec on the question these people will move out of New Quebec and on to the islands.
I have a suggestion to make if the federal and provincial governments insist on going through with their plan without consulting the Eskimo people. I suggest to the minister that the government consider payment in full of the expenses for removal of all their community property as well as their individual persons from their location in Quebec to any other place in the Northwest Territories-all of which is their home-to which they desire to move. That is regardless of whether one or 2,500 express the view to go. It seems that the fair and democratic thing to do is to hold a referendum among these people and find out their desires in the matter, rather than superimposing on their own personal feelings an arbitrary decision of the federal and provincial governments which has been dreamed up in concert-as the Winnipeg Free Press puts it, as an exercise in political appeasement.
The national unrest which this arbitrary action on the part of the government has caused-this typically Liberal arbitrary action of a Liberal government-is by no means confined to the province of Quebec or the province of Manitoba. In every centre of this country editorials have been written. One can pick editorials from any provincial newspaper condemning the action of the government in treating these people as human pawns. I should like to read an editorial in the Calgary Herald of March 3, the heading of which is precisely the phrase I have used- "Human pawns". The editorial commences in this way:
There is little justification for transferring jurisdiction over Quebec's 2,500 Eskimos from federal to provincial hands...
A meeting last week-
This editorial is dated March 3, 1964-
-between federal and Quebec authorities indicates that Ottawa is, after all, prepared to surrender to the demands of the Quebec resources minister, Rene Levesque, for the transfer of that province's Eskimo population to provincial authority.
Two sound arguments are advanced against this policy. The first is that-
-the Supreme Court of Canada ruled in 1939 that Eskimos were Indians and subject to federal jurisdiction. To turn them over to provincial jurisdiction is to be guilty of flagrant disregard of a judgment handed down by this country's highest court.

That is precisely what such a decision would mean; the government of Canada would be flying directly in the face of a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada.
Second, has sufficient consideration been given to the views of the Eskimos themselves? Last month, Quebec officials reacted in a somewhat petulant manner-
-a manner in which, I might add, the Minister of Transport ofttimes acts in this house when answering questions-
-when a federal spokesman suggested that a referendum be held to determine the Eskimo point of view.
Where is that referendum? Last August, for example, the Minister of Justice said, although not in so many words, that it would be held. He, like the disciple of the Secretary of State for External Affairs that he is, is becoming extremely proficient in skirting around direct answers to questions which are asked in this house. Both he and the Prime Minister have said, and not only on one occasion, that the Eskimo people will be fully consulted. That consultation, to be achieved in its fullest possible measure, should be consultation by referendum, not by merely explaining to the Eskimo people, as the minister of northern affairs put it on March 4, the terms and provisions of an agreement which has already been reached and decided upon and presented to the Eskimo people as a fait accompli. It is the fate of 2,500 Canadian citizens who have the federal franchise of which we are speaking here. They are people who are the direct responsibility of the federal government, not simply as a matter of constitutional law but because of the confirmation of their position handed down by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1939.
On March 10 the Minister of Justice was asked in this house a question by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm as reported at page 735 of Hansard:
When does the minister contemplate holding a sort of referendum, once the agreements are signed, in which the Eskimos would be asked whether they are in favour of that transfer?
The answer of the Minister of Justice was this:
Mr. Speaker, it is a question I would not like to answer without previous consultation with the other party involved in the discussions-
-namely, the province of Quebec: Not the Eskimo people; their feelings do not seem to concern the minister at all.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm asked this question a little later on, as reported on that same page:
Will the Minister of Justice meet the Hon. Mr. Levesque in this connection?

I suggest to the Minister of Justice that the matter of prime importance here is the feeling of the 2,500 Eskimo people. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is a very conscientious individual and takes his responsibilities seriously. He is given certain responsibilities under the act which set up his department, and one of those responsibilities constitutionally followed is that of caring for the welfare of the Eskimo people of Canada-not just those of any one particular province. I do not believe that he wants to see any transfer of jurisdiction. I think pressures are being applied from within his own cabinet by the Minister of Justice and by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to comply, for political purposes, with the demands being made by the province of Quebec. It is a shameful exhibition of complete surrender for political expediency and for the purpose of obtaining votes in the province of Quebec.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, the democratic process dictates that the Eskimo people themselves are the people who should be making this decision. The federal government is bound to care for the welfare and the administration of the affairs of these people by our own laws, as confirmed by a supreme court decision. They cannot all of a sudden slough off this responsibility simply because another province wants them to do so. The Prime Minister in the house, in answer to one of these questions the other day, said that all the provinces will be treated equally in this regard. This is another indication of co-operative federalism, where they want to come to one arrangement with one province and do nothing with regard to other provinces. This knife cuts both ways, Mr. Chairman. If there is to be a transfer of the jurisdiction of the federal government and administrative responsibility for the Eskimo people in this country, surely it should apply to all provinces; and this applies equally to administrative jurisdiction in matters concerning the affairs of the Indian peoples.
I suggest, sir, that there is a division in the cabinet over this question. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources deserves every assistance to see that the constitutional question here goes the way that it

It is the duty, I would suggest, of members on all sides of this house to support the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in insisting that the responsibilities which he is given under the act creating his department, and by the other laws of Canada, are carried out with regard to the Eskimo people and the protection of their rights. If the federal government is to insist on the transfer of the administration of Eskimo affairs, then I feel this house should insist that a referendum be held among the Eskimo people concerned so that their wishes are paramount here, and not the wishes of the federal government or the wishes of the government of the province of Quebec.
If the federal government arrives at the decision that it is a good thing, a desirable thing that the administration of the affairs of these people should be transferred, then they must, in keeping with the Prime Minister's undertaking in the house the other day, apply the same principle to the province of Manitoba, because there are Eskimos living in the northern portion of that province, as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources knows. It seems to me that one province cannot be treated in any different fashion than another; the principle upon which the transfer is being made must be uniform. I might just say, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Royal, I think it was, first raised the point as to whether this parliament would have the opportunity to consider any agreement that might be reached between the federal government and the provincial governments. There may not be time for another of our members to cover this point, but I would say that the hon. member for Peace River has raised this matter on a number of occasions, as well as the hon. member for Royal. I believe that if the matter is examined very carefully, it will be found that there is a

constitutional obligation on the part of the federal government to place any such agreement before parliament before it is given effect. I see the parliamentary secretary shaking his head in negation, but I believe that if he will look into this matter carefully he will find that the responsibility for the caring of the affairs of the Eskimo people is placed on the parliament of Canada and that respon-sibilility cannot be delegated until the parliament of Canada gives its approval-not the minister's department, because the minister certainly is not given that authority under the act which constitutes his department. I know that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources does not want to do that. He knows very well that the fair thing to do is to retain the responsibility for the care of these peoples in his own department. He is a conscientious individual and I know that he wants to discharge his responsibilities.

Well, I hope it gets the Eskimo people somewhere. I know that he wants to do the right thing because of his conscientiousness. He wants to ensure that the rights of these people are protected. Initially when he approached this problem, from reading the press reports I gather he was one of those who believed in a referendum, and I think deep down in his heart of hearts he still believes that a referendum is a proper way to approach this question, so that the views of the Eskimo people will be the governing views in this matter.
I can quite realize the pressure he must be under from his colleagues, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; but I say to him, "Disregard this pressure. They are not the important people, nor are the people in Quebec who are threatening and who are trying to insist on the transfer being made. The important people here are the Eskimo people themselves". This is one principle, judging from what I have been reading and hearing in this house, that the people of Quebec understand; that is, the principle of self-determination. They will be the first to stand up and insist on that right being enjoyed by all Canadians, from whichever part of the country they come. So I think that in order to clarify the matter once and for all, either the minister or someone in authority in the government should stand up and say that the government does not propose to proceed further with this matter; or indeed, if they do, the alternative is to hold a referendum in the democratic way so that the people most affected, namely the Eskimo people of New Quebec, will have the right of determining their own future without having changes

superimposed on their future lives and those of their children by government officials.

Mr. Chairman, primarily I should like to say a few words on the same subject on which debate was started yesterday by the hon. member for Northwest Territories and has been continued today by others. Before I do so perhaps I might be permitted to say how much I enjoyed listening to the remarks of the co-leader of the Ralliement Creditistes, the hon. member for Lapointe, especially his reference to certain television programs. I can only say to the co-leader of the Ralliement Creditistes that he convinced me for one thing, that if one wants to look for something sinister in anything he will be able to find it.
While we are on the subject of television programs may I say I was one of those who were enticed by the advertising by the Leader of the Opposition to watch the program "The Open Grave". I also took advantage of the occasion to watch the hour long program preceding it entitled "The Chief". I hope that someone on the government benches, presumably the Secretary of State who reports to the house for the C.B.C., will communicate my own thanks and I am sure the thanks of many other hon. members to the C.B.C., especially to the producer of the program, Doug Leiterman, and will commend that organization and Mr. Leiterman for producing such an excellent television program. They portrayed the Leader of the Opposition in a wonderful light, I think, and they did the job even better than Allister Grosart could possibly have done in his wildest moments. I am serious. I think it was an excellent program. I commend the C.B.C. for it and I hope that if they undertake incisive studies of other political leaders they will approach them in the same way.
With respect to the Eskimo and Indian problem in Canada I am sure it is well known that the New Democratic party and those of us who were formerly in the C.C.F. developed some time ago a program and concept relating to native Indian and Eskimo affairs that coincides precisely with the arguments we have heard today. We certainly welcome this late support and endorsation of the idea we have had for many years, namely that so far as government jurisdiction is concerned in relation to the Indian and Eskimo people the primary factor that should never be lost sight of is that they must be officially consulted and their desires must be heeded. This is of prime and paramount importance and we must never retreat from that position.
Some ten years ago the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and I sat in the legislature of British Columbia.

He was then leader of the Liberal party in that province. I am sure he does not need to be reminded and no doubt remembers precisely that in those years one of his clarion calls throughout the province of British Columbia with respect to the Indian people was that anything done in Indian affairs must be done with the consent initially of the Indian people themselves. That was his position ten years ago and I heard him expound on that idea in the legislature. I have read newspaper accounts of him saying the same thing throughout British Columbia and I hope he has not backed off from that position. Our guidepost in dealing with Indian and Eskimo affairs must always be that these people themselves should be the ones to decide initially, and not somebody else.
With regard to the particular matter under discussion, from what I have read about it and have gathered from listening to others it is evident that no group of Eskimos or no individual Eskimo made any approach to have jurisdiction over their affairs transferred into the hands of the government of the province of Quebec. The idea originated in the minds of people like Jean Lesage, Rene Levesque and others of their sort in order to satisfy some sort of inner craving for expression of their parochial ideals, and unfortunately they have dragged the federal government along with them. As a result the federal government has lost sight of the initial goal of consultation with the Eskimo people themselves. When I speak of the Eskimos I am also referring to the other group of original inhabitants of Canada, our native Indians, because the same thing holds true with respect to them. We must never lose sight of the fact that they are the ones concerned, that they should make the initial decisions and that the government should only be the agency to carry out what they decide should be done in the first instance.
Unless that is the case, then as far as I am concerned there should be no further negotiations with the province of Quebec or anybody else on the particular matter of transferring jurisdiction over the affairs of these people to the various provincial governments. I subscribe to the idea that as long as we maintain a constitutional structure that sets people apart on the basis of their racial background we are going to have two classes of people, one of whom is going to be considered second class or inferior. This has been the case with our native Indian people for many years. As long as we maintain one group of people under the jurisdiction of the federal government in respect of their civil rights, education and so on and the remainder of the people under the jurisdiction of the

Interim Supply
various provinces we are going to maintain and develop discrimination in favour of one group and against the other.
Our goal must be the transfer of jurisdiction but it must be done only with consent and after the people involved fully understand what is happening to them. The matter should never be negotiated at the top, as I gather is likely to be the case now, and a plan developed and presented to the Eskimo and native Indian people with the statement: This is the plan, here is our public relations explanation of it; do you want it or not? To do so places these people in the unfortunate position of having to make up their minds at a moment's notice on a matter that is most important to them when they have had very little opportunity to discuss it or to understand what is involved.
It is all right, I suppose, for the federal government to succumb to the pressures of a province, as has happened with this government, and to capitulate to threats or blackmail, if you want to call it that, on such matters as pension plans, taxation rights, the world's fair and a variety of other things, but in this instance we are dealing with the lives, the human rights and fundamental freedoms of people and we cannot possibly think of tossing these rights and freedoms away.
All sorts of suggestions have been made as to the approach that should be taken, but in essence I think this is what we would like to have the minister tell us. We would like to have the minister say to parliament that he is going to consult with the Eskimo people involved in this particular transfer to find out their views, their ideas and their opinions. On that basis he could then proceed to enter into discussions with the officials Of the province of Quebec, but first of all he should find out what the attitude of the people concerned is. If their attitude is that they are not interested in being transferred into the hands of Rene Levesque and others like him, then the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the government should stand up for the rights of these people, represent them properly and tell Rene Levesque to go to blazes. First of all let the government base its position on the desire of the people concerned.
Second, I think that in any event nothing should be done in this whole field of transferring jurisdiction over the original inhabitants of Canada until such time as we have had this dominion-provincial conference on Indian affairs, which I think will take place some time in May. This is the sort of place, with all the provinces there and with all the representatives of the federal government there, where we might be able to thresh out

a general understanding as to what course should be followed. Once there is some general agreement as to whether or not it is desirable to approach the native people on the question of transferring their jurisdiction, then we should go to the people concerned and say, "Do you want us to proceed or don't you want us to proceed?" We should outline the pros and cons, the benefits and drawbacks of such a transfer. Once the opinion of these people is ascertained, you can proceed with negotiations. If you do not consult with the people themselves first, what you will be doing will be selling their rights down the proverbial river. You will be disregarding the human dignity that everyone has and, unfortunately, you will be setting a pattern, whether or not that pattern is good or bad for all future discussions which may take place concerning the original inhabitants in Canada.
I just want to leave this one simple thought with the government. For heaven's sake do not do anything to jeopardize the rights of the people themselves. For heaven's sake go and consult with them and ask them first for their views, their ideas and, if necessary, submit a referendum to them. The situation should be explained thoroughly to these people, and you should submit yourself to the most incisive criticism and questioning by them. Tell them the truth about what is likely to happen and what is not likely to happen if jurisdiction is transferred. Let these people decide first what the government of Canada should do with regard to these negotiations, and then act like true, honest negotiators in representing them when you are dealing with the province of Quebec. If you do that first, you will have no complaints levelled against you. The people themselves will have no complaints because they will be the ones, initially, who started the whole process. Do not do it above, as has been the case so often in the past when governments have been dealing with the original inhabitants of this country; because if you make an agreement above, then you superimpose it on the individuals concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I only wish to make a few comments, before the resolution of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is passed and consideration is given to the interim supply bill which will probably be submitted to the house this afternoon.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) spoke a moment ago of the program presented last night over the English network of the C.B.C. and said that the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) could find something sinister in anything or anywhere, but, as I have not seen the program

myself, the only comments I heard were to the effect that the whole thing seemed to be a lot of publicity to promote socialist ideas which are overrunning the world. It is hardly surprising then that the hon. member for Skeena should be so interested in that play which was shown on the English network of the C.B.C. last evening.
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon we are again threatened with the sword of Damocles which was held over our heads on several occasions last year. Indeed, since yesterday, we have been told time and again that if interim supplies are not voted today, civil servants will not be paid, government bills will remain outstanding and the financial administration of the country will be paralysed. We wish to inform the Minister of Finance that we strongly object to this method used by the government to impose its decision on the house under the pretext that civil servants will not be paid and that the financial administration of the country will be paralysed if we do not adopt a certain piece of legislation at once.
The Minister of Finance does not even have to be here this afternoon to provide for civil servants' salaries and pay government bills. He just has to telephone the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Louis Rasminsky, and ask him to issue the necessary cheques. Then, everybody will be paid, since no Canadian bank will refuse such cheques unless the present Minister of Finance has completely lost our confidence.
Interim supply will probably include an important item, that is a short term loan, which means 91 days, bearing interest at 7 per cent. That loan to meet government obligations will amount to about $1.5 billion. At 7 per cent, that means an interest of $26,222,222.22 for three months. Twenty six million dollars in interest only on a temporary loan of $1.5 billion. And the government complains that it is short of credit, short of money and that the people do not want to invest in their country's development, whereas it is the government itself which tolerates a monetary system that is falling to pieces, a fact which is becoming more and more obvious.
Not so long ago, on March 24, the newspaper Le Droit published-not on the front page, because when news of that kind is made public, you find it most of the time near the obituary column, which goes almost unnoticed unless you happen to be interested-that news item which you find in the most hidden corners, the least interesting corners of any newspaper.
Here are, according to a report from Washington, the dangers of automation:
