A group of American professors, trade unionists and economists submitted to President Johnson a report in which they point out the dangers of automation.
Automation threatens to bring about in the United States unprecedented economic and social disorders, say the 32 signatories to the report-
Please note, Mr. Chairman, that I am not one of those signatories. Those are the views of economists, trade unionists and professors in the United States.
To go on with the quotation:
-among whom may be noted the Swedish-bom economist Gunnar Myrdal and Nobel prize winner Dr. Linus Pauling.
The report states the United States and the remainder of the world-
-this includes ourselves, here, in Canada. This also includes the Minister of Finance.
-will before long fall prey to a revolution which will bring unlimited production, thanks to machines, without the necessity of the co-operation of human beings.
So, means should be taken to ensure an income to all, the signatories to the report add.
Mr. Chairman, steps must be taken to guarantee income to all, not only in the United States but also in Canada.
We read in La Presse for Wednesday, March 25, 1964, an article entitled:
Means to be taken to relieve the poverty of 30 million Americans.
Thirty million people in the most wretched poverty out of a population of 200 million, while in Canada we have 500,000 unemployed, and if we consider an average of five individuals in each family, that would mean 2,500,000 people living in dire poverty. Besides, I would dare say that if we add to this figure all those who are not registered with the unemployment insurance commission, we could easily get the astonishing total of 5 or 6 million people, while the total population of Canada is 19 million. Six million Canadians are actually living in poverty in this country. Mr. Chairman, this is an intolerable situation.
On the other hand, the Minister of Finance tells us that the situation is improving. He tells us that only 5.5 per cent of the available labour force is unemployed. Five and a half per cent, in the public mind, does not mean such a large number of people. But if we take the trouble to consider the meaning of 5.5 per cent, we find that it represents more than 500,000 Canadian unemployed. That is the danger now existing in our country and the problem facing us at present.
How could an income be provided for everybody without accepting the theory advocated for many years by the Social Credit, namely the payment of a monthly dividend to each and everyone, so as to create the purchasing power called for by automation and to

Interim Supply
acknowledge that automation, instead of being detrimental to man, should serve his interests? That is what we want, what we are demanding and requiring of the present government.
Instead of racking our brains to find extravagant schemes like the winter works program -while machinery or power shovels are put aside to use men and give them some work why not use this program to make the equipment available to men, in order to help them rather than to enslave them? Instead of racking our brains, we should help organizations which are trying to look after people's leisure time. It would be so much more Christain and humane than to consider man like a beast of burden who must sweat and toil in spite of progress and actually be punished.
Mr. Chairman, it is this interim supply that is put before us at the very last minute, on Easter eve, and we are requested to accept it quickly. We are told: Accept, if you want to leave today for your Easter recess, accept it if you want to catch your train at 4.30 p.m. or your plane at five or six, or at eight o'clock tonight.
Mr. Chairman, we in this corner of the house are fed up with this sudden rush at the last minute. We no longer want that sort of thing for any consideration and for any minister. We no longer want the government itself to push us around or drive us into a corner, saying: accept that, or else we will sit tomorrow, holy Saturday, even on Easter day. We will sit as long as necessary.
We will no longer be pushed around like that in an endeavour to have us pass measures which should have been put before us perhaps two or three weeks before, so that all members of the house could discuss the subject matter, the advisability and the merits, in the minutest details, of everything that is not in the interest of the Canadian people.
Mr. Chairman, this interim supply will indeed provide for expenses. It will also provide for loans. As I said a while ago, when I called the attention of the Minister of Finance to that fact, all he has to do is what we suggest. The Bank of Canada should be used, without interest, when the bill is introduced, for the short term loan of 91 days and the $1 billion or $1.5 billion loan, so that we will not have to pay two or three times the amount of the capital. Let us pay the amount of the capital only. I do not mind that administrative expenses be charged to us but when, for example, we have to pay every three months $26 million in interest on those loans, it is a shame, it is like taking money from the pocket of the taxpayer.
[Mr. Caouette.l
Mr. Chairman, I have here newspaper articles saying exactly what we said during the last two sessions and during this one. I have here an article published in the Western Producer, on March 26, that is in this week's issue. It reads as follows:

For a long time purchasing power in the pockets of consumers has not been sufficient to buy the goods they need and which are available for consumption. Those who listen to "commercials" on radio and television need not be reminded of the savage competition among sellers for the buyer's dollar. They hear every day tempting offers with no cash down and ever lengthening periods to pay which competing firms dangle before the public in frantic effort to steal customers from one another.

We can read the following:

Time and again it has been asserted in these columns that a radical recasting of the monetary system is long overdue.

And that article by Mr. Waldrum was certainly not invented by the Social Credit organization, because the author is a man entirely outside the political scene; he just relates the facts as they are.
Here, in La Presse of Wednesday, March 25, we see that the United States have to deal with 30 million paupers.
The world is progressing; there is no better proof than the war waged against pauperism, as President Kennedy saw it, and which President Johnson is carrying on. A quarter of a century ago, it would have been taken for granted that this struggle meant taking the money from the "haves" to give it to the "have-nots". For until lately, indeed, it was presumed that the social cake was just so big and that the social problem consisted in sharing it.
Today, people here are preaching solutions as in the United States. They advocate certain remedies. These are the principal reasons for pauperism and distress. There are four categories of have-nots; for instance those whose proverty is due to lack of education.
Here, in this country, our young people have been urged for the last five or six years to go to technical schools, and become technicians, professionals. And, when they come out of those technical schools, when these young people of 20 or 22 years try to obtain a job, they are told that they lack experience.
When they have experience they lack education, and when they have education they lack experience.
That is the dilemma facing us.
Mr. Chairman, we do not go along with those pointless solutions which lead us nowhere. There is only one way to set up a practical economic order taking into account

the needs of the human person and that is to put the monetary sign directly in relation with the production the Canadian people are capable of. Then, we shall certainly have the liberation of the individual and the monetary sign will no longer be the master of the human person, but rather a servant, as we have been advocating for so many years.
Mr. Chairman, Social Credit would not do miracles and we do not need a Social Credit government to apply its plans. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), being an accountant, can understand Social Credit, but some circles around him probably prevent him from taking action. If he knew to what extent he would get the support of the Canadian people who are now in a dire situation, the Minister of Finance would not hesitate one minute more this afternoon and he would make an Easter present to each and every Canadian by calling the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Louis Rasminsky, instructing him to make available the billions of dollars needed for the good administration of Canada and the economic recovery in all Canadian provinces. Mr. Chairman, before I begin to make the statement that I wish to make on behalf of the Prime Minister, though perhaps the proceeding is a little irregular I am sure all hon. members will permit me to do what if my memory had been a little better I would have done at eleven o'clock this morning, and that is to congratulate the right hon. gentleman opposite on the 24th anniversary of his election to this parliament.
Hear, hear.

I well remember the day the right hon. gentleman was elected to parliament. It was on a Tuesday, and the fact that most of us are elected on Mondays makes this unusual event one of the things which have been unusual about his career throughout. I think we can all say without partisanship that neither parliament nor Canada would have been the same had he not been elected.
For fear of lapsing into politics, unlike my hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs who is absent, perhaps I had better get on with the chore entrusted to me by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister has asked me to make a statement which he regrets, owing to an indisposition, he is not able to be here himself to make regarding the transfer of duties between the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Forestry, a matter which was under discussion in the committee some days ago. I hope I will not be called to order if I follow pretty closely the notes I have, as I should like to carry out as faithfully as I can the mission entrusted to me.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested that the government had not complied with the provisions of the Regulations Act which require the publication of the order in council of February 3 made under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act. The hon. member knows, and I am sure all members know, that the Regulations Act does not apply to all orders in council. It deals with orders made-I quote from the definition of the act-"in the exercise of a legislative power". That act was passed

in 1950, when I believe the hon. gentleman was in the house, to ensure that the public would be informed of so-called delegated legislation. The aim was to make sure that parliament and the public knew what the law was as a result of the exercise of regulatory powers of a legislative character delegated to the government or to individual ministers. Orders in council under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act were then, and always have been since then, regarded as administrative orders since they affect the internal operation of government, not the rights and duties of the public; and therefore they have not been included among orders "of a legislative character" which have been published pursuant to the Regulations Act.
At the time the Regulations Act was passed the government prepared a consolidation of all the orders of a legislative character then in effect; that is, all the orders of the type which in future would be published. That consolidation did not include any orders passed under the transfer of duties act, although a number of such orders were in effect at the time. A further consolidation in 1955 also omitted any such orders. This same position was taken by the administration headed by the Leader of the Opposition when he was prime minister. In that period from 1957 to 1963, according to the information furnished to me there were 21 orders made under the transfer of duties act. Not one was published in the way which would be required if the Regulations Act was applicable; that is, by publication in the Canada Gazette. So far as the Regulations Act is concerned, the same practice has been followed by the present administration. While the present administration did not publish the order of February 3 and the subsequent orders because orders of the kind never have been published under the Regulations Act, the privy council office has readily made such orders available on request, as I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre acknowledged when he was speaking.
As to the content of the three orders in question, the Leader of the Opposition suggested that the order made on February 3 would have left the Minister of Agriculture largely bereft of his powers. I think that is a paraphrase of what the right hon. gentleman said. Such a statement ignores the fact that the Minister of Agriculture is responsible for the administration of over 30 statutes, not just for the three or four affected by the orders of February 3 and March 5.
Hon. members will no doubt recall that at the time the cabinet was reorganized the
Supply-Agriculture
Prime Minister announced that it was proposed to give the Minister of Agriculture the ministerial responsibility for the proposed branch lines rationalization authority which, if and when parliament has acted, will add substantially to his powers and responsibilities. It is true, of course, that certain responsibilities previously entrusted to the Minister of Agriculture were entrusted by each of these orders of February 3 and March 5 to the newly appointed Minister of Forestry. It is well known, Mr. Chairman, that the present government from the day it took office was committed to having two ministers associated with agricultural matters, one from western Canada and one from eastern Canada.
While the policy of this government has always clearly been that a minister from eastern Canada should be associated with some aspects of agricultural policy, it is not an easy matter to make a delineation of responsibilities which achieves that purpose -and I think that purpose has not been challenged anywhere in the house-and at the same time provides a good administrative structure.
The government decided some time ago that the core of the responsibilities to be transferred to the minister from eastern Canada should be those for rural development. But we also realized that this distinction could not be entirely clearcut. For example, it seemed to make sense that administration of the feed grain subsidy should be a responsibility of a minister from the eastern part of the country; but that is not strictly, if indeed it is at all, part of development policy. On the other hand, P.F.R.A. is essentially a matter of development and yet it is peculiarly a western concern. Farm credit is another marginal area; it has a lot to do with development, but it also has a lot to do with established agricultural undertakings.
The order in council of February 3 transferred five activities of the Department of Agriculture to the Minister of Forestry, but it did so on the assumption that the two departments would become organically a single department, with the Minister of Agriculture as the senior minister with final responsibility, and the minister of forestry and rural development with certain defined duties and functions in the field of agriculture. After the Minister of Forestry was appointed on February 3 it became possible to have more detailed discussions among all the ministers directly concerned and the Prime Minister. Both the Minister of Agriculture and the new Minister of Forestry quickly came to the view that they would

Supply-Agriculture
like to take a few weeks to work out the best arrangement of their functions.
Accordingly, it was decided not to implement the order of February 3 which had been prepared in advance of the new cabinet appointments. The order was at once withdrawn. The copies were called back. At that stage there should really have been a formal revocation of the order of February 3, which did not take place until February 20. That delay was occasioned by the pressure of other business, though the Prime Minister has asked me to say that he does not regard this as a sufficient excuse.
One of the problems which was being worked on by the ministers concerned was the question of the best administrative structure in the long run. They came to the view, and jointly proposed, that it would be best to have a division of functions and responsibility between two separate departments. That decision altered the earlier view of the appropriate division of functions. The number of transferred functions was reduced from five to three, P.F.R.A. and farm credit being retained by the Minister of Agriculture. Coordination of the work of the two departments was to be provided for, not by the organic linking of the two departments, as had earlier been contemplated, but by the establishment of an executive committee on agricultural policy consisting of three ministers-the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Forestry or, as the government hopes he will become when its legislative proposals are accepted by parliament, if they are, the minister of forestry and rural development -under the chairmanship of the Minister of Agriculture. These conclusions were put forward jointly by the two ministers, and as a consequence a new order was passed accordingly on March 5.
This decision was made with the full agreement of the ministers concerned. There was, of course, the technical error-and the government does not pretend for a moment that it was not a technical error-of failing to revoke the first order until February 20. It has been suggested that the government acted illegally in not following the transfer of duties prescribed in the order between February 3 and February 20. The government has been advised that, as a matter of law, no member of the public would be or would have been adversely affected as a result of the Minister of Agriculture doing anything which, under the order, the Minister of Forestry could have done. The Minister of Agriculture did in fact sign eight ARDA agreements with the provinces. I understand they were with two provinces, Ontario and 
Nova Scotia. The validity of those agreements, like any other external act of the government, is covered by the protection that the law and jurisprudence afford in cases where there may be a technical defect in the authorization of anyone holding a public office. For greater certainty the government would be quite prepared to have the Minister of Forestry also sign the ARDA agreements to which I have referred.
Of course, public money was spent during those 17 days. It was spent under the authority of parliament. It was subject to all the normal checks of any public expenditure. There has been a suggestion that funds may have been spent illegally. Funds have been appropriated by parliament from year to year for ARDA, maritime marshland rehabilitation and other purposes involved in the recent transfer of functions. When funds are appropriated by parliament for a purpose, their release is subject to a great many rules. These rules are made under the Financial Administration Act and they prescribe the precise kind of authority that there must be before an expenditure can be made. They are not, for the most part, provisions of law; they are provisions of administration. They are internal requirements adopted so that administration can proceed, but with full safeguards.
What undoubtedly happened and what probably has happened in every case of a transfer of duties, and I emphasize "in every case", is that an expenditure may have been made under authority granted by the minister formerly responsible after the authority had technically been vested in a colleague.
I am glad to be able to assure hon. members that a check has been made and that there was no expenditure authorized by the Minister of Agriculture personally in the period from February 3 to February 20 in any of the areas transferred by the order of February 3 to the Minister of Forestry.
There is one other possibility. An official in the Department of Agriculture might, in those 17 days, have authorized an expenditure of the kind he could deal with under the authority he had received from the Minister of Agriculture after he should have had a new authority from the Minister of Forestry.
The government is advised that this frequently happens for a week or two after transfers of duty are made. The business of government goes on while the necessary consequential changes are being made. I could give an example in another case.
According to the best advice the government could get, it would appear that the suggestion that any law had been disregarded is not well founded. Orders in council under the transfer of duties act have never been

published before under the Regulations Act, and the 17 day delay, while a technical error, is one that does not involve illegalities any more than it may have done in similar situations, and there have been many of them, in the past.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to speak at length after the kindly reference to me at the beginning of the hon. gentleman's remarks. I am not at all suspicious and it may well be that these well intended and sincere good wishes may have been in the contemplation of the hon. gentleman. However, I do thank him and the members of the house. Twenty four years is a long time and it was after many endeavours to get into this house that I finally succeeded. All I can say is that the spirit shown today in the words of the hon. gentleman is entirely consonant with that which I have found in the house at all times. Sometimes I have been known to disagree with those sitting opposite, but at all times recognizing, I hope, the fact that the House of Commons is a great club in which friendships are built up irrespective of disagreements that take place from time to time. The Minister of Agriculture has not been here very long, but after he has been he will find that this is a place in which the amenities are practised despite the asperities that sometimes pass between us.
Having said that, I now come to the subject matter of the exculpatory epistle by the minister in respect of a series of errors that cannot be brushed off as merely technical mistakes. These are serious errors. These are things that indicate the government is new to its responsibilities and to the need of carrying out the statutes and laws that are in effect. In this regard there has been a serious departure. Indeed, the Montreal Star, which I have never regarded as one of the major supporters of the Conservative party, had this to say in an editorial:
What is one to make of a government which gets as tangled up in its administrative traces as the Pearson government in Ottawa? Who is doing its planning and how is it being run? The confusion surrounding the functions to be allotted to forestry minister Sauve is to be cleared up shortly by the Prime Minister himself but the memory of a month at cross purposes will remain.
Sir, we used to hear of bumbling and bungling. The postgraduates in these arts who sit opposite. I doubt that there has ever been a series of errors and mistakes so consistent in so short a time as we have seen since the present government took over.
On February 3 the Minister of Agriculture was, to use the words that the minister quoted, bereft of many of his responsibilities. No doubt he will say that what happened was entirely satisfactory to him. After all, if you are not discharging your responsibilities losing
Supply-Agriculture
them does not cause you much concern. It has been an interesting division. The Minister of Agriculture, with wide experience in that field has for some reason or other had his powers and authority trifurcated. On February 3 he lost ARDA, P.F.R.A., which has always been in the Department of Agriculture and should be nowhere else, farm credit, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act Administration and the administration of freight assistance for western feed grains. He lost all of them under one order in council. A few months before he had the wheat board removed from him.
Stripped to the bone.

One after the other these very important adjuncts of the Department of Agriculture were removed from him, and there he stood almost naked of responsibility except for a number of statutes that were referred to a moment ago.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: That is the bare truth.

But the important things were removed, transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce, transferred to the Department of Forestry. A kind of troika was set up. I know that three heads are better than one but as one coming from western Canada, it does strike one that with his capacity he could very well have discharged these responsibilities. Yet they were removed from him. Why? Was it a matter of his effectiveness? Was it because he felt that someone else should look after these matters? We do not know. All we know is that the press has stated that there has been a power struggle going on. If there has been a power struggle, all I have to say is that the Minister of Agriculture did not have any of the power.
What has happened? On the 3rd of February these things went from the Minister of Agriculture. An order in council was passed. The Minister of Transport is an expert on the privy council. He occupied the clerkship of the privy council. Yet today, in all seriousness, he advances the argument that, after all, nothing took place but a technicality. He said the government decided that the order in council of February 3 should not be proceeded with and they withdrew it. How can they withdraw anything that has received the approval and consent of His Excellency the Governor General? He says they merely wished to change their minds, but he knows better than that.
I did say it was an error, did I not?

Oh, an error; it is more than an error. It is a colossal example of the

Supply-Agriculture
negligence that characterizes too frequently the actions of the present government.
Well, from the third to the seventeenth, we-
I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to make an error; it was the twentieth.

Well, the hon. gentleman had more than three days of grace. For 17 days, the hon. member for Calgary South went about this country as Minister of Agriculture, denuded of his major powers. I doubt whether he knew anything about it. It is said, however, on responsible authority that a power struggle is taking place. I want to be fair. The minister gave an interview on March 20 in Calgary and he said this;
We have had no arguments about this. We could not afford to have arguments. We are only a minority government. 11 we were to fight, we would not be there.
Well, that is sound reasoning. All I can say about that is that for 17 days he acted as a minister, carrying out responsibilities that had been removed from him. I need not add any more in that regard. It shows the slip-shod methods, the short cuts through parliamentary requirements and responsibilities, the denial of the rule of law that, while regarded as casual by the Minister of Transport, seriously challenge the responsibility of a government that would permit such things to happen.
On the twentieth, the order in council of the third was cancelled. The minister has said, as I understand it, that there was no expenditure of money made during those 17 days under the direction of the Minister of Agriculture.
I think perhaps the right hon. gentleman would want to have it technically accurate. I said one authorized personally by the Minister of Agriculture.

I can see the distinction the minister has in mind. We want to find out what orders were made during the period from the third to the twentieth that were signed by the Minister of Agriculture in respect of this department, authority over which he no longer had.
I gave that in my statement. I think I said there were eight ARDA agreements signed, four with Ontario and four with Nova Scotia.
Does the minister say nothing else took place?
That is all of which there seems to be any record.

I think the first thing the government will have to do will be to

have the Minister of Forestry sign those agreements, otherwise they will not be effective. I think that there should be an explanation of what took place on the twentieth, for from February 20 until March 3, was it, another order in council was then passed. What happened during that period of time? Once the Minister of Agriculture was denuded of powers and they were transferred to the Department of Forestry, unless there was an explicit order in council retransferring those powers to the Minister of Agriculture, the mere abrogation on the twentieth of the earlier order in council would not be effective. I think they will have to pass an order in council to ratify what was done. Indeed, when they have done that they will have to come before the house and ask, and they will receive-ask and ye shall receive- forgiveness for what they did and legalization for what they ought not to have done.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the government perhaps deserves to be congratulated upon the honesty of the statement that has been made on its behalf today by the Minister of Transport. I think that, particularly in the last few sentences used by the Leader of the Opposition, the proper treatment has been given to the government for what it has done. Even so, Mr. Chairman, I believe that one or two things might be added, and that I might be permitted to add them because of the points that I raised on orders of the day when we first learned of these errors, to quote the Minister of Transport, that were made by the government.
Some of us on this side of the house made a number of statements that might have been called charges or allegations, and some of them the Minister of Transport admitted today to be correct. We contended that once the order in council of February 3 had been passed, the government had no legal right not to put its terms into effect. The Minister of Transport has now admitted that but says it was only a technical error. He says the order in council should have been revoked right away instead of leaving it there for 17 days. At least, he has now admitted the correctness of the charge that was made from this side of the house.
I remind him of an occasion when the previous government was in power when it, too, forgot to pass an order in council amending a decision that had been made. The then member for Bonavista-Twillingate thought this was a case of fumbling, or whatever term it was he applied to the government of that day. This was the occasion when the previous government, by order in council, appointed Hon. Earl Rowe as lieutenant

governor of Ontario. Hon. members will recall that the first order in council not only-appointed Hon. Earl Rowe to that position but fixed the date on which he would begin his new duties. Later, the then government decided to change the date, I think it was by exactly one month, but for some days or weeks the then government forgot to pass an amending order in council to change that date. As the Minister of Transport will recall, this was drawn to that government's attention in an interesting way, and it corrected its mistake by quickly passing an order in council amending the previous one.
No harm was done by this error or oversight in the intervening period, and all that happened was that a news report was not substantiated by an order in council. At any rate, the present government realizes it can make the same kind of mistake that the former government made. It too can delay by forgetting, if you will, to pass an order in council it ought to pass.
But the main point about what I am saying in this portion of my remarks is that the government has now admitted what we contended when we raised this matter on orders of the day, that the government had no legal right-just because the ministers decided it between themselves-not to put into effect the provisions of order in council P.C. 1964-157 of February 3.
Another point we made when we complained about this was that there was a 17 day period during which there was a possibility some of the acts of one or other of the ministers might be illegal. At the time it was contended that we were making wild charges, but in his statement today the minister has admitted that this was a possibility, to the extent of saying some of the acts, orders and expenditures have been checked or are being checked. The minister has also admitted that the government is prepared, if necessary, to get another signature on some of the agreements that were signed or to take any validating action that may be necessary.
As I say, this simply adds up to a confirmation of the point that we made, that there was some question about the legality of actions between February 3 and February 20, 1964. Even though we are treating this matter today in the friendly mood one would expect, after a confession on the part of the government, and after the kind of words the Leader of the Opposition has used on this, the 24th anniversary of his first election to the House of Commons, a day some of us remember very well, we must not overlook the seriousness of what is before us. If the rule of law means anything, then surely the people who should be most zealous in carrying it
Supply-Agriculture
out are those who make up the government of the day. We hope, as a result of this experience, this kind of thing will not happen again. However, the trouble is that it is too often we have to stand up in the house and say we hope this sort of thing will not happen again, yet it goes on happening.
The other contention that was made by me-I do not know if others made it-was that the government should have published the orders in council of February 3 and February 20 in the Canada Gazette, part II. The Minister of Transport gives two reasons by way of defence for this not having been done. On the one hand he says it never has been done in the past, that orders in council under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act have not been published in the Canada Gazette, part II. The other defence he uses is that the language of the Regulations Act refers to orders in council having legislative effect.
I would like to deal with that second point for just a moment. It is quite true-in fact I read this portion of the Regulations Act-

Could I ask the hon. gentleman a question. The hon. gentleman, who is very assiduous in all these matters, was here in 1950 when the Regulations Act was passed. He was here when the original consolidation of the statutory orders and regulations was made. He was also here when the revision of the statutory orders was made in 1955, and during all that time a great number of orders were passed under the transfer of duties act. They were never put in the original revision; they were never put in the revised document and were never published at any time and, since there were 21 in a six year period, there were probably at least twice that many in the whole period since then. In view of that, does the hon. gentleman think that now suddenly a change should have been made from the practice that was followed, going right back to the passing of the Regulations Act?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I shall deal with that, but first may I confirm what the Minister of Transport has said, that I was here on all those occasions to which he referred. In fact I have a volume of the 1950 Hansard in my hand and I shall be quoting from it. I shall not be quoting from myself, but there are things in it to indicate that I took part in that debate, and I remember it very well. But may I interject at this point to say that the fact it has always been done a certain way does not necessarily mean that is the right way and that it is in conformity with the law.
It may be that this incident is the kind that tests the practice, and brings out the

Supply-Agriculture
fact that perchance the practice has not been in conformity with the law or with what was the spirit and intent of the law.
It is clear, as I was about to point out, that the Regulations Act defines a regulation for the purposes of the Regulations Act as:
-a rule, order, regulation, bylaw or proclamation (i) made, in the exercise of a legislative power conferred by or under an act of parliament, by the governor in council-
-and so on. Section 6 of the act says:
(1) every regulation shall be published in English and in French in the Canada Gazette within 30 days after it is made.
I should like to take a minute to dwell on the word "legislative." The act says:
-a rule, order, regulation, bylaw or proclamation (i) made, in the exercise of a legislative power-
The minister seeks to draw a line between legislative and administrative functions, and I suggest that may be a line which the government has been drawing without the right to draw it in the way it has done.
I have checked each of the four statutes to which reference was made in the order in council of February 3, the Agricultural Farm Credit Act, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation and Development Act, the Rehabilitation Act and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. In each of those statutes, in words enacted by parliament, it is prescribed by legislation that the minister means the Minister of Agriculture. Parliament in its legislative capacity so ordered.
The effect of order in council P.C. 1964157, as is the same with subsequent orders in council in this field, is to change a fact that was determined by parliament, to change a situation ordered by legislation. By virtue of this order in council these four acts were changed and the minister, instead of being the Minister of Agriculture, became the Minister of Forestry. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in effect that is the exercise of a legislative authority, that it is actually a case of legislating, and that the government does not get around this by calling it administrative.
I recognize that there were 21 of these orders in council during a six year period referred to that were not published, and it may be there were many more during the years the Liberals were in power. But I should like to read to the Minister of Transport a portion of what the then prime minister, Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, said on June 12, 1950, as reported in Hansard at page 3497. This was on the occasion when we were passing the Regulations Act, under which we still operate. We were dealing with the definition, a portion of which I have just read, and Mr. St. Laurent said this:

With respect to this definition, I want to state again that we found it would not be possible or prudent to make statutory exemptions with respect to the application of this statute. We wanted it to include everything, to make it necessary for us to call attention to anything that was not going to be governed by it. So we said we would make it as sweeping as possible so it would apply to every kind of order that has legislative effect, made under authority given by parliament; and if we wanted to take anything out of that general, sweeping declaration we would have to call attention to what we were taking out so if there should be any controversy as to whether it should be in or out the matter would be brought to the attention of hon. members and the public.
In other words, Mr. St. Laurent was dealing with three things-the definition, section 6, which calls for publication, and section 9 which permits a special order in council to exempt certain other orders and regulations from publication. The whole spirit of the legislation as presented to us on that occasion was that the inclusions were to be of a sweeping nature comprising everything that had legislative effect or was done in the exercise of legislative authority unless the government felt something should be omitted, in which case there had to be a special order in council exempting that class of order from publication.
I have not been able to find any indication of any order in council which exempts from publication orders in council made under the provisions of the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act. It may well be that a mistake has been made during the years in not publishing orders in council made under this act, but the statutes of Canada are quite clear. Members opposite say, in the case of the four statutes we are talking about, that the changes made in the status of the Minister of Agriculture were only administrative, that they did not have to publish the orders in the Canada Gazette. I grant that there was no deliberate concealment. The matter got into the newspapers and, once we learned about them, the orders in council could be obtained by asking for them at the privy council office. But, for my part, I did not know of their existence until I read about it in a newspaper.
Let us say that there is no case against the government of deliberate concealment, but the failure to publish this kind of order in council means that for a period of time the law of Canada has been changed by the cabinet. I suggest the argument that this has not been done over the years since the new method of procedure came into being does not justify the government's failure to comply with the appropriate statute. It certainly does not justify this particular example. I think what we have gone though now makes it clear that the pattern ought to be changed and that orders in council passed under the

Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act ought to be published in the Canada Gazette so that there may be no question but that these things will be found out.
This is an embarrassing situation. The government felt happy that it was not obliged to publish this, so that it would have time to sort things out. But parliament depends upon the operation of the rule of law in a matter such as this. I join with the Leader of the Opposition in saying that if the government finds, on further consideration, that it needs some legislative enactment to cover the errors, then because of the spirit of contrition in which the Minister of Transport has come before the house we shall be forgiving, and pass any such enactment. But I hope that as a result of this experience a little more attention will be paid to the niceties of keeping the law, because not just niceties are involved in this question, but the whole question of the rule of law itself.

May I ask the hon. member a question, to fill in the time between now and five o'clock? When the hon. member referred to section 9 of the Regulations Act he used an argument which I had in mind. He said he was not able to find an order in council which did, in fact, exempt any regulation or class of regulations. Do I understand him to say that no such order in council was passed, or that notice of such an order was not published?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I said I know of no order in council under section 9 exempting from publication orders in council passed under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act. Oh, there are a number of orders in council under section 9 passed to exempt certain classes of order in council from publication. The best example of this type of thing was given by Mr. St. Laurent, as reported on the same page of Hansard from which I was quoting earlier, when he talked about orders given from time to time from the control towers at our airfields. These would be multitudinous. There are orders in council under the section excepting that class of order in council or regulation from publication.
Again, I think the government acted as it did simply because it believed this was an administrative matter. I think it was both a mistake and a contravention of the clear terms of section 6 of the Regulations Act.
Can we be assured there were no penalties of a quasi-judicial nature imposed by these regulations? If there were, I think they could be seriously challenged.

To the best of my knowledge-and I can assure the hon. gentleman
Business of the House
that a very careful search has been made by people much more competent than I am to do so-there was nothing in that category at all.
Progress reported.

Mr. Chairman, earlier we were discussing the activities of the government under the transfer of duties act in transferring certain responsibilities from the Minister of Agriculture. I would suggest that they would do Canada a much greater service if they were to transfer some more duties from the Minister of Agriculture, namely his function under the Cold Storage Act as that act applies to fisheries products.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: We could put the Minister of Agriculture in cold storage.

My colleague says that we could put the Minister of Agriculture in cold storage, if desired. That is something the government will have to consider, not me. But I would earnestly appeal to the government to consider my request and would point out that we used to put forward this point of view years ago when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was merely the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and not a member of the cabinet. I would ask him to take up the cudgels while he is in cabinet as he used to when he sat on this side of the house, in order to get some decent and fair consideration for fishermen under the Cold Storage Act. Right now they are being completely swamped with the situation that exists in agriculture, and no fair or reasonable consideration is being given to the requests and desires of these people for subsidies and subventions under the Cold Storage Act for purely fisheries products. If the government would take that course and make another transfer of duties and exclude the Minister of Agriculture from dealing with this matter, I am sure we would be much better off.

I would just like to comment on this matter, Mr. Chairman. In so far as cold storage is concerned, we have taken a very close look at every application we have received and most of them have been approved. Hon. members will remember that the previous government had an austerity program and

cold storage grants were frozen; but I suggest that we have approved more applications in the last few weeks than were approved in the preceding 18 months.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman, there is one thing I should like to mention in connection with what has been said this afternoon. I think hon. members of the house will be interested to know that so far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned, we are interested first in farmers across Canada and the job we can do for farmers. ARDA has been mentioned many times in this house, and I would like hon. members to know that although perhaps we have not talked about it very much, since May 1, 1963 until the present time the government has spent a little over $11 million on ARDA projects. The previous government, from the inception of the act on June 22, 1961 until the time I was appointed Minister of Agriculture, had carried out $2,185,000 worth of projects. I might say that since May 1 we have completed over five times as many ARDA projects, in dollars as the previous government.
I think I should possibly say something about feed grain because this is a very important matter to eastern farmers. Hon. members will recall that on August 27 we changed our feed grain policy whereby we would pay the storage on feed grain at eastern spots, and we would also pre-price the grain and provide the same price as applied to China or anywhere else. As a result of this policy we found that on March 12 we had 47 per cent more feed grain on spot in eastern locations than we had a year ago; that we will not have to bring one bushel by rail, and the prices have been stabilized. I do not have the most recent figures, but from the middle of October until the middle of February there was no substantial change in price. I should also perhaps mention something about farm credit.
Mr. Chairman, could I ask a question at this point?
Yes.
Has the minister the figures right now of the price of, let us say last October, 1963 and the price of January, 1964 or February, 1964, on oats and barley? Does the minister have those figures?

I could obtain them in a moment for the hon. member. I had that information at noon. There have been some changes up and down, but for the most part there has been no change in price. The fact that we have had the grain on spot is responsible for some stabilization in so far as price is concerned. On March 14 we had 21 million bushels of oats, wheat, barley and corn in eastern locations, and this will be ample to

take care of the feed requirements of eastern Canada. As I pointed out before, this is 47 per cent more than was in eastern locations just a year ago.
With regard to farm credit, Mr. Chairman, some people think we have not done anything in this connection. I would like hon. members to know that from April 1, 1962 to March 31, 1963 the number of loans serviced was 7,438, for a total of $90,924,000 lent by the Farm Credit Corporation; and from April 1, 1963 to February 29, 1964 we serviced 8,613 loans for an amount of $106,708,000. It is perhaps well for hon. members to know at this time that I was in complete agreement with the changes so far as my department was concerned. Personalities were not involved at all. We asked ourselves, "What is good for agriculture? How can we better serve the farmers"? That was the only thing we had in mind.
Hear, hear.

My department has over 30 acts to administer and employs something over 10,000 people. Taking ARDA away from the department will reduce that number by eight or ten employees, and as far as the administration of feed grain is concerned, not more than one employee will be affected in this transfer. So I will lose possibly eight or ten people from my staff of 10,000. I know that ARDA is very important as far as farmers are concerned. I think this is exemplified by the fact that our government believes in it; we believe it is a good act-the early planning of it goes back to 1955-and since May 1, 1963 we have done five times more than was done by the previous government.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I could pose one question to the minister about cold storage activities. I think the minister said that in the last few weeks they have approved more applications under the Cold Storage Act than were approved in the previous 18 months. Did I hear the minister correctly?

This figure may not be too accurate; I do not have the exact figures here and I would not want to mislead the committee as far as this matter is concerned. We feel that more thought should be given to the question of cold storage, because I personally do not believe that the grants are doing the big job that is required today with regard to cold storage, We have apples to think of, fish, vegetables and all these things, and it seems to us that there should be some change in policy. Nevertheless we are giving careful consideration to the applications that come to us. We are considering them on their merit so we can do something in this regard

where co-ops and people are going to be affected, until such time as we have an opportunity to present new legislation which will include a change of policy which we think will do a better job for all those in need of assistance across Canada.
Has the austerity program been rescinded or is it still in effect?
They wouldn't know what it is anyway.
This program is partially in effect. As I said, we are considering each application on its merits.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to say a few words first about the statement made by the Minister of Transport on behalf of the Prime Minister on the point that I raised originally in this house with regard to the possibility of the illegality of any action taken by the government between February 3 and February 20. My first reaction to the rather lengthy statement of the minister was rather one of great disappointment. Hon. members will recall, I am sure, that we made quite a to-do about this and many questions were asked in the house. We asked for a strong opinion as to the legality. We felt it was necessary for this house to be reassured that any actions taken by the government during that period were legal, and I suggested that remedial, retroactive legislation would have to be introduced.
The statement read by the minister certainly contained no strong legal opinion. In fact, there were one or two suggestions in it that led me to believe that the legal advisers could go no further than to suggest that the government might get away by bringing in the word "technicality" and by making statements such as no member of the public was affected by anything done in this period. If this is the sort of statement that the government is going to make in order to try to whitewash this matter, if the government is going to give us a nebulous statement of this sort instead of the candid opinion we have asked for, then I am sure the house has to inquire a little further.
I noticed yesterday that the government asked to stand two motions by the hon. member for Provencher, under notices of motions for the production of papers. These items dealt directly with action that could have been taken during the period in question and if that information was before us we would be able to determine for ourselves just how far the government has to go to patch up the series of blunders that occurred during this period. I found also that I was more than a little shaken by the effrontery of the government with regard to the manner
Supply-Agriculture
in which they deal with their duties, and the way in which they regard orders in council. An order in council is passed which has the force of law. It affects departments that are very important and the attitude of the cabinet seems to be that it does not matter what the law is, that it does not matter whether the action is legal, that they will do what they like, fix it up somehow and push it through.
I should have liked to hear further assurance from the minister than just that he would have the Minister of Forestry sign these eight ARDA agreements. I may not be the best lawyer in the house but in my opinion this may not take care of the legality of the situation at all. I do not believe the Minister of Agriculture had the authority to sign those agreements. In other words, they are not in effect now, and that is not a mere technicality. Complete absence of authority cannot by any stretch of the imagination be called a technicality. The Minister of Agriculture had no authority. These agreements are not in force in law and I do not think the signing of them now by the Minister of Forestry will give them legal effect.
We would like to hear from the minister that he is going to bring in retroactive, remedial legislation at the earliest opportunity. I know it is a little difficult to conceive of the government bringing it in this evening. Right after Easter would do. I was also somewhat shocked by the suggestion of the house leader that these estimates have to be passed tonight. I remember asking the Prime Minister on Monday to discontinue the budget debate. Once the budget was presented to the house there was no need to carry on with the very general budget debate.
The government knew quite well that it had to have interim supply. The government now says that these estimates have to be passed, but if that is so they also knew that before. Despite requests from this side the government persisted in continuing with the budget debate on the first two days of this week. In my opinion it again shows the government's contempt for parliament that they will unnecessarily spend two days on the budget debate and at the last minute come on their knees and say that these estimates have got to be passed.
This attitude makes me somewhat fed up because there was a speech I very much wanted to make this afternoon on interim supply. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources referred to me this morning rather gratuitously and rather unfairly, I thought, and the speech I have had ready for two weeks waiting for an opportunity to deliver it is still resting here. I want to make that speech on northern affairs because I
