think it is very necessary that the minister take a little instruction. But in order to assist the government and because I thought it was necessary to pass interim supply I sat and said nothing. I am prepared not to have the opportunity to make the speech before Easter, if that is necessary, but if the government thinks it is going to get these estimates passed before the house adjourns for Easter, then all I say is I am sure we will be back here next week, not because some members are stubborn, not because they refuse to cooperate, but simply because the government has taken the high-handed attitude that it is going to handle things the way it wants to and members are going to do as they are told by the government.
The steamroller.

It has never been my opinion that the government is mightier than parliament and this is one time that we had better show the government it is not. I trust the government will content itself with the knowledge that these estimates are not going to be passed before Easter. If they had any honest belief that they should be passed before Easter, then they should have brought them in at a time when essential and necessary measures should have been discussed instead of insisting on proceeding with the budget debate.

Mr. Chairman, I had no intention of speaking this afternoon but I see that the Minister of Agriculture is in the saddle. I also speak as one who represents a constituency which is very much interested in agriculture, and I do not feel I should let this opportunity go by without saying anything. We have been accustomed to listen to the Minister of Agriculture tell us that everything has been bright and rosy since he has been the minister, but I should like the minister to come with me and consult the agriculturists and farmers of my riding and also the agriculturists of the whole of Canada. If he did so he would indeed find that their story is different from the one he tries to put across. I have before me a clipping from the Manitoba Co-Operator of February, 1964, and contrary to what the minister would like us to believe prices are going down rather than up under his efficient and able direction. I should like to refer to the average price for good slaughter steers for 1962 compared with 1963 on the Toronto market. For 1962 good steers averaged $25.65 whereas in 1963 under the minister's able leadership they only averaged $23.65 per hundred pounds. What about hogs, grade A, Mr. Chairman? In 1962 the average price for grade A 
hogs was $29.60 whereas under his great leadership they only averaged $27.80. And so on.
It was music to us a while ago to hear the Minister of Agriculture say that ARDA was a great law and that it was the hope of the agriculturists and farmers of Canada. But he went on to say that the credit for it should go to the Liberal party. You and I know, Mr. Chairman, that the ARDA program was instituted under the leadership of the Leader of the Opposition and also with the co-operation of the then minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who is now, although he is in the opposition, on a trip abroad selling Canada and the products of Canada. Let it be known to the whole country that faith in agricultural policies was never greater than when the Conservatives were in power from 1957 until 1963.
The Conservatives were the ones who gave the farmers hope. We were the ones who instituted the stabilization act which was a general charter for farmers and permitted our farmers to know in advance from year to year the prices they would receive for their products. This measure gave our farmers some hope, and it was instituted long before the hon. member for Calgary South became the Minister of Agriculture.
I should like, Mr. Chairman, to refer to what the occupants of the treasury benches promised during the campaigns in 1962 and 1963 in order to deceive the farmers and in order to capture power. I have in front of me a pamphlet issued in 1962 in which they promised the farmers a minister of agriculture for eastern Canada. Where is that minister of agriculture? They have retreated on this matter just as they have on many others. They have been going backwards rather than going forward as our farmers would like them to do. One of the first things they did when they assumed office was to take away the 25-cent subsidy which was given to the producers of milk all across Canada. What was the effect of this action in my riding, as well as in the province of Quebec? During the time we were in office the total amount paid to farmers in Quebec under this subsidy program was about $21,800,000. In my own riding, the total subsidy payment was $1,576,000.
I should like the Minister of Agriculture to come to my riding and try to sell the farmers the idea that they are more prosperous under the leadership of the Liberals than they were under the leadership of the Conservatives. I should like him to come to my riding and go from farm to farm asking whether they prefer the leadership of the Conservative party or of the Liberal party. I am sure the answer he would receive would be that the Liberals

were trying to take away what our farmers deserve. I could not let this opportunity go by without asking the Minister of Agriculture to re-establish this subsidy. It would not be a big chore for the government to back up because it has been backing up ever since it came into office. The government is always putting forth legislation and then taking it away. Once more I would ask the minister finally to accept the fact that the farmers want this 25 cents per hundred subsidy on milk re-established.
I am speaking here on behalf of my fellow farmers in the riding of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. I want nothing more or nothing less than the best that can be obtained for the farmers of my riding and the farmers of Quebec. I am imploring the minister to re-establish this 25-cent subsidy because I am telling him he is the cause of the farmers in my riding losing thousands of dollars. I think it is my duty to bring this matter to the attention of the government. Even if I have to get down on my knees to ask for the re-establishment of this 25-cent subsidy for the benefit of my farmers, I would do so.

I am always trying to catch up on things that have happened here in the past, and in his remarks the minister referred to the fact-I was not completely clear on this-that in the year 1955 the government of that day, I presume a Liberal government, had done something or created something or was involved in something like ARDA. This is a complete mystery to me and I think the minister having raised it should satisfy our curiosity and interest.

In answer to the hon. member I may say that I was referring to the Senate committee on land use. It was as a result of the findings of that committee in so far as rural rehabilitation was concerned that this program was developed.

This is delightful. I know the minister is relatively new to federal politics, but this is the first time I have heard that the Senate committee on land use had anything to do with the development of ARDA. I think I am one of the few members who has read the proceedings of that committee carefully.
I do not come from an agricultural or farming riding. All one has to do is to look at the Laurentian shield and you know why. We have a tremendous area of cut-over forest land or what might be called settlers' areas. This is a problem that rims all the way from northern Ontario through Manitoba and Saskatchewan and, certainly, it is very prevalent in Quebec. One of the reasons those of us from these areas were so enthusiastic
Supply-Agriculture
about the ARDA concept was that at last we had a program that offered a marriage be-twen forestry and agriculture, and a program that could go into those regions where far too much of the forest had been eliminated, in so far as agriculture was concerned, to suit the wishes and needs of bygone generations.
I may tell the minister that we were involved in a committee on lands, forests and waters a few years ago and also in a committee on agriculture, and both of these committees came forward with suggestions which I might refer the minister to, and which predated the introduction of ARDA. In so far as the Senate committee on land use is concerned, I recall that they brought in experts from all across the country to express opinions but they did not take the trouble of crystallizing all the evidence and offering recommendations. Perhaps the minister is suggesting that all the time the officials of the Department of Agriculture were moving toward the ARDA concept, as a result of what the Senate committee on land use was uncovering. This would be sensational if it is factual. Again I cannot believe it because I know how difficult a time the previous government had selling the ARDA concept to the officials of the Department of Agriculture. One of the reasons the minister can stand up and take credit for $11 million under his regime, in contrast with only $2 million under the previous regime, is just because of that lack of enthusiasm on the part of the permanent officials of the Department of Agriculture.
The minister made the point that he did not lose many people in the way of employees by the slough off of ARDA to the Minister of Forestry. This proves the point. The Department of Agriculture and its senior officials never had any great enthusiasm for ARDA. That is one of the reasons why the program has crept and limped along. At the time he lost his portfolio due to the last general election, the previous minister of agriculture was working up a pretty heavy head of steam and temper about the response from the department, and for the minister to come in here and give the impression he is bulling ARDA through to greater success is much more than I can take.
This is neither the time nor the occasion for the rebuttal of the partisan hyperbole which the minister engaged in, but I do not believe any minister of the crown should be allowed to get away with that kind of stuff in this chamber. I suggest that due to the different things which have happened in the last month or so, despite the way they happened, we have at last got an imaginative program like ARDA not only out of the hands

Supply-Agriculture
of the officials of the Department of Agriculture but out of the minister's hands, and that that is good.

Almost any day, Mr. Chairman, I can pick up a paper and see where a lot of wind has come from some corners. I am hearing a little more of that wind today. I would like to assure the hon. member that it is something to talk, but it is something else to do things. All I am saying is that we are doing something with ARDA. We are not just talking about it, like it has been talked about this afternoon.

I have been waiting for some months to reach the Department of Agriculture estimates and I am very pleased to see the minister here today, apparently quite ready to take on all comers and answer a few questions. Dealing first with the Farm Credit Act, I would like to know how many loans would have been made to farmers if those loans had not been arranged at 5 per cent by the previous administration?
Further, it takes a great deal of time to process all loan proposals. It took our administration time to process them, and I would suggest 50 per cent of the loans for which the minister has taken credit were already well processed by the time he took office.
I am glad to see that the minister supports the farm credit program. It loosens up credit all across the nation, and has made it possible for the family farmer to get on his feet. I can only compliment the minister on supporting this program.
In his public utterances the minister, time and time again, has suggested that all the problems of agriculture are well in hand.
Hear, hear.

You may well cheer, but see if you cheer when I finish. It is fine for people who have had good crops and who had grain to sell under the imaginative sales program which we launched. They have sold their grain at good prices, but what about the people who did not have crops? They are the people who need crop insurance, and I want some action taken in my province through co-operation between the federal government and the Alberta government to see to it that the small farmer who does not get a crop has some security.
In my district of Athabasca we were not fortunate last year. We did not have a great crop and the people there do not think all the problems of agriculture are solved. They are looking for something like the acreage payments they used to get. They got them three times in three bad crop years and it saved them. It may be that some of my colleagues have sympathy with rich farmers. I know the

Minister of Agriculture has, but the people I am talking about think that $200 to buy underwear for their children is important. If they do not get acreage payments they will want to know why. They need this kind of help.
I am pleased to see that the price of hogs has not fallen to disaster levels. It is always possible that it may reach the danger point. I am not going to blame the Minister of Agriculture for this, but I suggest he should not wait to do something until it reaches disaster levels.
I am personally in favour of the hog quota. I have never believed in supporting hog prices across the board, but I do believe in a reasonable family farm quota, and if prices continue to slip I suggest that the minister lower the hog quota to 75 and increase the support price to 25 cents a pound. If he looks at the statistics over the past five years he will see that, from the time our administration introduced this scheme, it has not cost the people of Canada one cent in deficiency payments. Before that it used to cost them from $23 million to $24 million a year to support hog prices. I suggest that the minister should not forget the lessons of the past. He should lower the quota when there is a danger of overproduction and lower prices, and raise the price which the small farmer gets.
I can say the same thing about the grade A hog bonus, and I suggest the minister look at the statistics showing how many grade A hogs were raised due to the sensible program of supporting the price of grade A hogs with the $3 bonus. With the price per pound that the farmer gets, and with the addition of the grade A bonus, it makes all the difference to him.
If the Liberal government has no program for agriculture, and I have reason to believe it has none, I suggest it take the advice of the farm unions. We took the suggestions made by the farm unions and they were put into effect by our minister of agriculture. The problems of agriculture have only been scratched, but to come to the question of the ARDA program-
Are you speaking of the Hon. Douglas Harkness or the Hon. Alvin Hamilton?
I am speaking of our whole agricultural program. The stabilization prices act was introduced by Hon. Douglas Harkness.
Then give him credit.

I have no quarrel whatsoever with our program from the time we took office. It was imaginative and the people of Canada know it was effective. The present minister is very proud of our wheat sales,

but I ask who made the breakthrough? Who promised the $2 wheat? We promised the $2 wheat and we produced it for the western farmer by selling the wheat we had. Look at the record. I have been consistent. I have always pressed for the sale of wheat to China, or to anybody else who wanted to buy it.
Now I want to speak about ARDA. It is a program I back, and I do so for this reason. I am a federal member of parliament. I am not only the member for Athabasca in Alberta but I represent every farmer in Canada, and the ARDA program will give the same kind of hope to the eastern farmer that the western farmer has now. I repeat that the western farmer's problems are not over by any means, but the ARDA program will give to the small eastern farmer the same kind of hope we have established west of Winnipeg. Let us give the credit for ARDA to whom it is due. Maybe the Liberals dreamed about this program quietly, but it was our administration which put it on the statute books.

Mr. Chairman, I would have many things to say on the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), but I find the situation we witnessed last year is still the same this year. Before the Christmas recess, we studied the estimates of the Department of Agriculture on the last day, and this year we study them at the last moment.
It seems the government intends to submit the estimates of the Department of Agriculture only when we have very little time to discuss them.
We would have much to say on the Department of Agriculture, and more particularly on the needs of the farmers.
At the present time, in eastern Canada, and especially in my province, farming papers contain editorials to which I would like today to call the attention of the house. I would mention in particular the editorial published in the newspaper Terre de Chez Nous on March 19, 1964, which was entitled:
Look out for fancy skating, Mr. Pearson.
And then we read:
Agriculture up for auction in Ottawa.
This well indicates the way our eastern Canada farmers and those of the province of Quebec understand the agricultural policy of the present government.
Some time ago, I put to the minister a question concerning ox and calf hides.
Nowadays packers and farmers sell such products at 6 cents a pound, that is $2.50 or $3 for an ox hide and about 75 cents for a calf hide.
Supply-Agriculture
I asked the Minister of Agriculture a question on that point, and he answered in these terms:
The problem is, Mr. Speaker, that we are eating in the neighbourhood of 6,000 head more cattle, so we have 6,000 more hides, and the population has not increased enough to absorb them in the use of leather goods.
That was the reply by the Minister of Agriculture.
Later on I received information from the Department of Trade and Commerce to the effect that in 1962, there were 2,452,320 oxhides in the market in Canada, as against 2,462,996 in 1963.
Besides, if we refer to page 942 of Hansard, we find out that the price for cowhide, on the Canadian market, was 14.4 cents in 1963, compared with 13.8 cents on March 1, 1964.
Since I raised that matter on February 24 last and again on March 16, I would ask the minister if he can explain immediately why farmers and packers in my area must accept a price of 6 cents a pound when the market price, according to the Department of Trade and Commerce, is 13.8 cents a pound.
Also, I should like the minister to tell us, in view of the fact that the question was put to him on February 24, why farmers and packers in my area and in my province have to accept a price of 6 or 7 cents a pound for calf hide, when the Department of Trade and Commerce tells us that the market price, on March 1 last, was 20 cents a pound.
The minister can see that there is a big difference and he will understand that the farmers want to know why that price is much below the price I got from the Department of Trade and Commerce. Moreover, the minister maintains that our production is too high, and that there is no market for all those skins in Canada. He says that our exports to the United States and other countries are higher than our consumption.
Before going further, I am asking the Minister of Agriculture to tell me whether he has considered the problem and why the farmer does not receive the actual market price for his ox and calf skins.
Mr. Chairman, I am asking that question to the Minister of Agriculture, I asked the same question on February 24 last and I would like to know now whether he is in a position to answer today.

I do not know. I cannot answer this question, and I am sure no one else can answer it. The law of supply and demand enters into these things and the hon. member's particular problem may be a regional problem. But I will be glad to look into it. This is the first time I have heard of it.

Business of the House [Translation]

I asked that question on February 24; that was almost two months ago.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I have permission to draw to the attention of the house the fact that unless, somehow, we have unanimous consent to proceed, then otherwise, under the rules this house will have to sit tomorrow, Good Friday, a course with which I personally would not agree. I therefore suggest that we give unanimous consent to carrying on with government business-that we should not adjourn at six o'clock tonight but that we carry on with government business as long as possible in order to see what advance can be made.

I point out immediately that the understanding was that there would be an adjournment, provided interim supply were passed. We passed interim supply. There never was any question that before the adjournment for Easter recess the supplementary estimates were to be passed. At no time was there such an understanding.
Here we have before us $240 million of supplementary estimates. Every session parliament is criticized for the precipitate pace with which it approves the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars without examination. Our responsibility is to carefully examine them. That responsibility is not discharged when a government proceeds as it has during the past few days. On Monday and Tuesday it proceeded with the budget debate. There was no reason in the world for that course unless the position of the government was that these supplementary estimates did not have to be passed.
Let me point out, Mr. Speaker, what took place in this house on March 23, as reported in the translation of the remarks of the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) at page 1358 of Hansard. The hon. member asked:
Could the Prime Minister publish a notice showing the holidays of secretaries-
And so on. Then there is text by the Prime Minister underneath as follows:
I thought it had already been indicated to the house that it is our hope and intention to adjourn Thursday evening and resume our session on April 6. There is one reservation to that, of course, and that is on the understanding that interim supply is passed by the house.
Now, that was the understanding, but it went further than had been the case on an earlier day; and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) commented:

No, you did not say that the other day.
Then the house proceeded to give the government interim supply, as it should, because we have the fullest opportunity to examine expenditures. But to suggest that the house is to be browbeaten by the proposition that unless we concur and vote hundreds of millions of dollars we are going to sit on Good Friday is one which I say will not be acceptable to the people of Canada-let that be clear. This cannot be justified. As a matter of fact, I doubt whether the house could sit on that date without unanimous consent, although I will not say-

Might I ask the right hon. gentleman a question. I do not know whether the right hon. gentleman caught the statement made by the house leader, which was that under the rules of the house we are bound to sit tomorrow at 11 a.m. unless there is unanimous consent to change the rules. The house leader said that he did not want to sit tomorrow, and I do not think any of us want to sit, but we will require unanimous consent to prevent us from sitting because there has not been 48 hours' notice.
Mr. Speaker, this sort of-
Blackmail.

I will not use the word I have in mind. This is an endeavour to bamboozle the house and force us into a position where we vote hundreds of millions of dollars without examination. I say that there is no necessity for the passage of these supplementary estimates at this time; they can be passed after we return. It is not a question of holding up salaries because we have passed interim supply. I am beginning to realize now what the plan was-to waste the time by having the budget discussed. I am using the phrase "waste the time" in the sense that the time should have been used for discussion of the supplementary estimates.
The government now come along and say that we are going to sit tomorrow. The very suggestion that we sit this evening for a couple of hours and pass $200 million worth of supplementary estimates is a travesty of parliament, let me make that clear. We are not going to be placed in the position of being the puppets of those people over there who have not properly organized the business of the house.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with part of what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) said we are in agreement. We are in this jam, and it has to be called that, because the program announced by the government on February 28 for the period up to Easter was later changed. On February 28 the program of business was outlined. It did not

include the budget. It was putting into that program not only the presentation of the budget but several days of budget debate which upset the schedule and put us in the position in which we find ourselves at this time. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I think we should act as mature people and face the fact that this kind of thing frequently happens and that we do get to a place where certain necessities have to be met.
The Leader of the Opposition has read the answer of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to a question about another matter to support his contention that we were never told that the supplementaries have to be passed before the end of March. It was my understanding all the time that both interim supply and supplementary estimates had to be passed before the end of the fiscal year, but even if that understanding is not clear it seems to me it is the tidy thing to do. It seems to me that we have been bedevilled for a couple of years with estimates which have been dragging on which we have had to pass after the event, and it would be a good idea, if parliament wants to do things in a businesslike way, to get all the estimates for the fiscal year 1963-64 out of the way before the end of that fiscal year. In other words, I think we should put the blame, as it should be put, on the government for changing the program and putting us in this jam; but as a parliament I think we should face the fact that something must be done and that we should decide without passion or a lot of emotion what we are going to do. If the Leader of the Opposition feels it is useless to sit tonight and that we cannot do all this in two or three hours, then that is a statement of fact and let it be put that way. I submit we should face the facts of our job and that we had better come back on Monday and Tuesday and try and finish it then.

Mr. Speaker, we are against any attempt by the government to use force and threats in order to hasten the passage of supplementary estimates. However, we do not think it is logical to delay their passage, since we shall have the opportunity, when the budget debate is resumed, to criticize the government about certain pieces of legislation we do not approve, along with other parties. If the official opposition is unwilling to allow those estimates to be considered more rapidly, it is merely to put grit in the bearings and not for some serious reasons, because they are well aware that they will have every opportunity to consider those supplementary estimates on resumption of the budget debate.
The members of our group do not want to prevent passage of those estimates and will 20220-97J
Business of the House
readily agree to any compromise proposed so that they may be passed as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, we do not agree, as I said earlier, to pass the supplementary estimates speedily and accept anything as if it were a mere pittance.
We are ready to sit tonight. As for sitting tomorrow, we object for several reasons. If we had to come back Monday or Tuesday, we are quite ready, but not without knowing exactly what the government requests. I find it hard to understand that we should always be placed in that situation. It was the same when the Conservative party was in power and now when they blame the Liberal party for acting this way, it is an indication of their lack of responsibility.
Anyway, we are prepared to co-operate, but not to pass in a lump sum all the estimates without previous scrutiny and consideration.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to the attention of the house that we now have under question the word of the Prime Minister of this country. This is not something that has come upon us suddenly. On March 11, as is reported at page 778 of Hansard, you find the heading "Business of the house" and then, "Announcement of Easter recess". Then there are the words of the Prime Minister as follows:
I informed the house the other day that today I would announce the plans for the Easter recess. It is proposed, Mr. Speaker, that the house should adjourn at the end of business on Thursday, March 26 and reassemble on Monday, April 6.
The business is not completed,

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Then, as has already been drawn to our attention, the Prime Minister of this country reaffirmed that position on March 23, and although the question that brought forth his answer was on another subject, nevertheless his answer referred to the adjournment of the house, and I repeat it. These are the words of the Prime Minister:
Mr. Speaker, I thought it had already been indicated to the house that it is our hope and intention to adjourn Thursday evening and resume our session on April 6. There is one reservation to that, of course, and that is on the understanding that interim supply is passed by the house.
That is the word of the Prime Minister of this country. Everybody has made plans and arrangements based on that. With regard to the business of the house, we have gone through this time and time again, session after session, but we are not pressed at this particular moment to effect what the hon.

Business of the House
member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) calls a "tidy operation", passing $240 million in just a few hours.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I made no such suggestion. The hon. member knows that I suggested we pass these items in this fiscal year, and I suggested that in view of what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) said, we come back and do it decently and properly on Monday and Tuesday.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Hansard will indicate what was said. The organization of the business of the house failed because of the obstinacy of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) insisting on having his budget discussed rather than dealing with these other matters, which are also his responsibility, namely the supplementary estimates. There are no salaries involved here. These are debts owed by the crown and can be settled in due course. But to ask us to continue and to sit on Good Friday or on Easter Monday is contrary to the given word of the Prime Minister.
May I also draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that two years ago the Liberal party of this country, in the person of their then house leader, Hon. Mr. Chevrier, requested that the house should not sit on the Thursday before Good Friday because he said it is a holy day. I drew this to the attention of the present Prime Minister and asked him to look back at Hansard for April 12, 1962, page 2894, when Mr. Chevrier put forward that proposal. The Prime Minister said he would look at it, but he did not report on it. At that time the prime minister of the day, Right Hon. Mr. Diefenbaker said that under no circumstances would the house sit on the holy day, and consequently we did not sit on the Thursday before Good Friday, at the request of Mr. Chevrier. Now the present group are asking us to sit on Good Friday.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this just cannot be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -I shall not allow anybody to distort my words-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -and try to suggest that I even implied that this house ought to sit on Good Friday. I said clearly that I disagreed with that proposition, and this was why, to circumvent the rule or to modify the rule, for that particular purpose I said we would need unanimous consent. I said exactly the contrary of what the hon. gentleman has contended.
What about holy Thursday?

Mr. Speaker, did the
minister imply that in order to avoid that we would have to sit tonight and pass the supplementary estimates that are before us?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend's speech, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to continue with my question of privilege. If the hon. gentleman from Winnipeg South Centre has finished, I would ask your permission to answer the allegation that there was, or would have been, an agreement to adjourn to April 6 as soon as interim supply was passed. Nobody should allow the words of the Prime Minister of this country to be put in doubt. When the Prime Minister referred to that reservation first, he was expressing a hope; and second, he stated so after I had at least once, if not twice, announced in the house that the house would be proceeding with supplementary estimates first, and then with interim supply. It is clear that when the Prime Minister said that, that he implied-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -that these matters would both be dealt with first.
What a weak argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I now suggest, Mr. Speaker, that under the reserve of having to sit on Monday, if we must, but to avoid sitting on Good Friday, this house do not adjourn and that it sit tonight until the house decides on an adjournment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
You break the Prime
Minister's word.

Mr. Speaker, if it is necessary to have unanimous consent to avoiding sitting tomorrow, feeling as I do about the way the government has mismanaged the business of the house, I am giving notice now that the only way I will give consent to avoid sitting tomorrow is that this house adjourns now until April 6, and on no other condition will I give my consent. If the government does not want to sit tomorrow, that is too bad. I want the Prime Minister's word kept, and the only condition upon which I will give consent, in order to avoid sitting tomorrow, is on that basis.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters).
Mr. Speaker, I would like to call it six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In the absence of any order of the house, if we adjourn at this point, then of course according to the rules of the house we will resume tomorrow at eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in order to avoid-
Six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -having to sit on Good Friday, I suggest that the house give unanimous consent to adjourning until Monday, March 30, at 2.30 p.m.

No.
Business of the House
Refused.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Since there is obviously not unanimous consent, this house stands adjourned until tomorrow morning at eleven o'clock.
It being twenty one minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.

FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE (March 31, 1964)
Proposed Agenda and Procedures
A.	Proposed Agenda
1.	Relations between shared-cost programs and fiscal arrangements, including the implications of contracting out.
2.	Canada pension plan.
3.	Reciprocal arrangements regarding taxation of government departments and agencies.
4.	Other aspects of fiscal relations.
5.	Federal proposals regarding loans to university students.
6.	Liaison arrangements, with particular reference to calendar of meetings for 1964.
7.	Report on Canadian 1967 world exhibition.
8.	Other matters.
B.	Proposed Procedures
All provinces agree that the procedures adopted at the November conference were generally satisfactory and should be followed again at this conference. There will be an opportunity at the opening of the conference to discuss such possible changes and improvements in these procedures as might be considered desirable.

March 31, 1964
The opening meeting of the conference will be held in the legislative assembly at 10:00 a.m. on Tuesday, March 31, 1964. Termination date of the meetings will be established by the conference.
Places will be available at the main conference table for the Prime Minister of Canada, four of his ministers, for the

premiers of the provinces and one minister of each province. A section will be set aside for other delegates.
Delegations
A list of the members of the federal delegation is attached hereto. The list of the provincial delegations is being compiled and will be issued in a supplementary release.
Proposed agenda and procedures
The proposed agenda and procedures will be issued in a following release.
Opening statements
Since this conference is a continuation of the federal-provincial conference held in Ottawa last November, it is anticipated that most delegations will not be issuing an opening statement.
Interpretation
As in the case of recent federal-provincial conferences, simultaneous interpretation, in English and in French, will be provided in the main conference room.
Official functions
1.	On Tuesday, March 31, the prime minister of Quebec and members of the cabinet will receive the Prime Minister of Canada, provincial premiers, ministers, delegates and news representatives at a reception in the Chateau Frontenac at 6:30 p.m. Dress: "Lounge Dress".
2.	On Tuesday, March 31, His Honour the Lieutenant-Governor of Quebec, will receive the Prime Minister of Canada, the federal cabinet ministers, provincial premiers and ministers at a dinner at Bois-de-Coulonge at 7:30 for 8:00 p.m. Dress: "Black Tie".
3.	On April 1, a reception for delegates will be held in the legislative council chamber at 12:30 p.m., followed by a luncheon in the parliamentary restaurant at 1:00 p.m.
Coverage Arrangements-Press, radio, t.v. etc.
Still, television and newsreel photographers will be admitted to the main conference room at 9:30 a.m., March 31, to prepare for general photographic coverage of the formal opening of the conference. Picture taking will end at 10:15 a.m. sharp.
Official photograph
An official photograph of the heads of delegations and delegates to the conference will be taken in the legislative council chamber at 12:15 p.m., Tuesday, March 31. Accreditation
Special press passes will be required for admission to the conference area. These passes will be issued on arrival in Quebec city.
Facilities-Press, radio, t.v.
The conference press room-rooms A-81 and A-85-(the legislative assembly private bills' committee room) will be equipped with telephones, typewriters and cloakroom facilities. This room is for the use of all news representatives, accredited to the conference, except those from Quebec who will use their regular facilities in the legislative assembly press gallery, t.v. production room, room A-198; press conference and briefing room, room A-199; press office, room A-80; press enquiries during the conference sessions should be directed to the press office in the legislative assembly building (as listed above). Tel.: 693-5268 or 693-5269.
A press working room will be available in the Chateau Frontenac hotel for the benefit of out-of-town news representatives.
Canadian National and Canadian Pacific telegraph facilities are permanently located in the legislative assembly building. Arrangements for filing will also be available in the press room at the Chateau Frontenac hotel.
Travelling arrangements
In co-operation with the executive of the parliamentary press gallery, a chartered Trans-Canada Air Lines aircraft will carry members of the press from Ottawa to Quebec city, on Monday March 30.
In order to provide sufficient time for research and filing, the aircraft will depart from the T.C.A. Uplands terminal at 11.45 a.m., arriving in Quebec city at approximately 1.00 p.m. Lunch will be served on the aircraft. Ground transportation will be provided from Quebec airport to the hotel.
Because of airline regulations, T.C.A. advises all passengers must obtain tickets prior to the aircraft's departure. The charter fare (including ground transportation in Quebec city) is $20 return.
Tickets may be obtained, upon payment, from James B. Regan in the Prime Minister's office. Cheques should be made payable to T.C.A. Hotel accommodation has been arranged for all members of the press at the Chateau Frontenac, where members of all delegations will be staying. Rooms will be assigned on arrival.
